title: Data Analyst Skills You Need for Your Next Promotion
content: Introduction Let me start off by acknowledging that this subject has been written about and discussed repeatedly on many different platforms. So, what could I offer that hasn’t already been said? Well, as it turns out, I’m a lot older than the average Medium author. Although some people politely refer to me as "mature" or "experienced," the truth is that my perspective is shaped by the fact that I’ve been around long enough to remember when neon colors and gradients on bar-charts were cool.

title: Data Analyst Skills You Need for Your Next Promotion
content: Therefore, what I can offer you is advice that stands the test of time. Data Visualization As an analyst, you will probably spend at least 10 times as much time analyzing the data as you will have to present the information to your audience. Therefore, graphics and other visual representations are important because it creates a better understanding, even for those who aren’t trained in analyzing datasets. By building visualizations, you can help your company’s decision-makers understand complex

title: Data Analyst Skills You Need for Your Next Promotion
content: ideas at a glance. So how do you improve this skill? Well, there are plenty of training options in the form of online courses and plenty of tools specializing in visualization. However, I’m hesitant to recommend specific technology or course because the world changes so quickly, and I want to offer advice that stands the test of time. Therefore, make a habit of exploring other people’s work. Build a bookmarks folder called "Inspiration" and fill it with blog links. Dedicate 15 minutes weekly to

title: Data Analyst Skills You Need for Your Next Promotion
content: browsing the blogs to fill your brain with possibilities. I also recommend buying a couple of books. Edward Tufte is the grandfather of Data Visualization, and I’m also a fan of Nathan Yau over at FlowingData.com, where you can find books, blogs, courses, and tutorials. I keep both of his books, Data Points and Visualize This, on my bookshelf for inspiration. The mechanics of how you will actually create the visualization will come with practice. Some of you will fall in love with R or python,

title: Data Analyst Skills You Need for Your Next Promotion
content: and others with Excel or Tableau. The key is having your brain filled with possibilities, so you can imagine what you want before you build it. Data Cleaning Data Scientists are known for their claim that "80% of building a machine-learning model is preparing and cleaning the data." However, this is also true for data analysts. Whatever the actual percentage, the truth is that a large proportion of time spent with data, in general, is spent cleaning it. Cleaning data is important, because

title: Data Analyst Skills You Need for Your Next Promotion
content: uncleaned data can produce misleading patterns and lead to mistaken conclusions. Early in my career, I was tasked with delivering the percentage of support calls that were resolved on the first try. As I walked my management through the results, one of them insisted that the numbers "didn’t make sense." When I did more research, I discovered that the calls data had a column called "status" that sometimes was populated with an "X." Apparently, the system would record an "X" for a test record,

title: Data Analyst Skills You Need for Your Next Promotion
content: which should be ignored. Data cleaning skills grow with hands-on practice and business expertise. This makes it difficult to accelerate. In general, sites like kaggle.com or zindi are not the best places to practice data cleaning because they are focused on data science, and the datasets are usually pretty clean already. On the other hand, government websites such as https://data.ca.gov/ or https://data.gov/ are a great place to find datasets that are messy. You can also follow the TidyTuesday

title: Data Analyst Skills You Need for Your Next Promotion
content: project, even if you’re not an R user, to find interesting datasets and get familiar with the types of cleaning steps that occur in the wild. SQL As I mentioned, I am hesitant to recommend a specific tool or technology because of how quickly the landscape changes. It is probably safe to say that python and R are here to stay, but SQL is on another level. SQL is the language of databases; therefore, learning SQL will always be the most direct way you can manipulate and study datasets for your

title: Data Analyst Skills You Need for Your Next Promotion
content: analysis. If you work at a company that lets you download extracts in excel sheets – ask around to see if it’s possible to access the database directly with SQL. Once you are comfortable with database structures and writing SQL to get the data represented in the way you want, your efficiency will increase along with the quality of your work. Many resources are available to help you improve your SQL game, CodeAcademy, Udemy, and Udacity are great free resources for finding hands-on courses. SQL

title: Data Analyst Skills You Need for Your Next Promotion
content: Generator and SQL Beautifier are great links to keep handy that will help you learn. Stack Overflow has a great community for answering technical SQL questions if you get stuck. Edit: The SQL Generator by Rasgo no longer exists – Rasgo has transitioned to using AI instead of SQL Generator templates. Critical Thinking Critical thinking is one of the hardest things to grasp as there are not many courses or a one size fits all approach to mastering this skill. Critical thinking is a conscious

title: Data Analyst Skills You Need for Your Next Promotion
content: effort to challenge the automatic mental processes that rule over us. Critical thinking isn’t something you naturally have or something that once you get it, it’s always "on." Instead, critical thinking is something that you consciously activate whenever you have an important decision or analysis. It is a purposeful effort to challenge, question, and confirm hypotheses. While there are many different resources available to help you improve critical thinking skills, the one I want to focus on is

title: Data Analyst Skills You Need for Your Next Promotion
content: asking questions. If you get into the habit of writing down lots of questions, you will engage in critical thinking. Let’s pretend that you were asked to look at customer churn and whether it has been improving recently. Stop to ask yourself questions, such as: How is churn calculated? Why that way? Are there other ways? What is churn, from the perspective of the customer Is it always a customer’s choice? What factors might matter? Can I measure those? What is the goal of this task? Prove,

title: Data Analyst Skills You Need for Your Next Promotion
content: disprove, demonstrate, support? What could I be overlooking? Are there known assumptions I can’t validate/prove? Notice how this line-of-questioning forms layers upon layers. Answering a question might lead to more questions. That is perfectly fine. That’s the point! For example, when I was an analyst at a Telco, I was asked to look at potential reasons why churn suddenly increased in the prior month. (it was currently April). I used critical thinking by writing down a list of questions similar

title: Data Analyst Skills You Need for Your Next Promotion
content: to the above list. When I got to the question about how churn was calculated, I challenged myself to consider if there were other ways to measure churn. Long story short, I discovered that: The company used "end-of-month" numbers to calculate churn The month of March was actually a "fiscal" month that covered February February was the shortest month of the year Using an alternative formula for churn showed that the rate did not increase in March Basically, the formula for churn was such that it

title: Data Analyst Skills You Need for Your Next Promotion
content: would "spike" during the shortest month of the year, which was called March, just simply because of how the math worked. The moral of the story is that critical thinking sometimes takes you to conclusions you would not expect. It is also something that you can decide to improve upon today; it is not some mythical soft-skill that you need to be born with! Communication Communication on the other hand, is a soft skill. You might be the most talented and insightful data analyst the world has ever

title: Data Analyst Skills You Need for Your Next Promotion
content: seen, but it won’t do any good if you can’t communicate with others. And by others, unfortunately, I mean non-technical people. As an analyst, you straddle two different worlds. In one world, you must address technical points with your peers and other data experts. In the other world, you are a translator for business-centered decision-makers. You need to provide clear, high-level explanations in a supportive rather than confusing way. One way to start exercising this soft skill is to get

title: Data Analyst Skills You Need for Your Next Promotion
content: involved in a community. There are many online communities, websites, and forums for data analysts to get involved in. I’m a big fan of slack and discord channels as a way to interact with others, but those are known to die off quickly. I have found Locally Optimistic and DataTalks.Club to be a good consistent place for analysts to hang out. You should also practice your communication skills by starting a blog. Medium is a great place to get started, where you can exercise your creativity and

title: Data Analyst Skills You Need for Your Next Promotion
content: practice, practice, practice. Conclusion It is still important to follow the latest trends and skill-up on things that make you marketable. For example, 20 years ago VBA, macros, DAX, and ASP were great skills to give you an edge towards promotion. These days, those skills are less likely to matter. Hopefully I’ve given you some helpful advice about skills that haven’t changed in the past 20 years, so you can avoid getting lost in the weeds. If you ever want to reach out to me and discuss the

title: Data Analyst Skills You Need for Your Next Promotion
content: old days, you can find me hanging out in Locally Optimistic and DataTalks.Club, and you can always ping me directly at Rasgo.

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: The Great Resignation is the perfect time to leave your unfulfilling career behind to become a data analyst. Never before has there ever been such a mass exodus of people looking for better opportunities that encompass room for advancement, flexible working conditions, respect in the office, and fair wages. With so many individuals looking for a fresh start, it’s no wonder that many of them are looking to the alluring world of tech to provide the change they need. Data science, analysis, and

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: engineering are maintaining a foothold as some of the most sought-after jobs for those looking to make a career change. While you may think that the three disciplines mentioned above are the same, they differ significantly in their qualifications and job duties. For those looking to make a quick switch to a different field without having to spend years studying, becoming a data analyst may be the right fit. Data analysts are gifted with the ability to tell a story using data. Taking existing

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: data, they use tools such as SQL, Excel, and data visualization tools (such as Tableau) to produce visualizations and reports that describe in laymen’s terms the current landscape of the data. Job duties include determining business problems, pulling data from databases using SQL, conducting analyses and producing visualizations using Excel and visualization tools, and developing reports that present the findings of the analysis for stakeholders. Simple coding skills in R or Python may also be

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: required depending on the job, and simple mathematical skills in arithmetic, algebra, statistics, and probability are standard. With data analyst positions treading the line between a new challenge without having to spend years in school, it’s a no-brainer for those looking to make a career change. The Roadmap Background Most roadmaps toward any data-focused position or career change are often so extensive that they would take a couple of years of full-time study to complete. The average worker

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: takes 11 months to plan a career change, leaving most of these roadmaps out of touch with what people need. Furthermore, external factors, such as the amount of savings and life commitments, can make it impossible to complete a career change in an amount of time that is feasible for most, leaving many to stay at their previous jobs. Considering all of these factors, this roadmap has fine-tuned the process of becoming a data analyst into seven short phases that can be completed as quickly or as

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: slowly as necessary. Remember, to make a career change you only need to know enough to get a job. In-depth learning can take place on the job once you have satisfied the basic requirements and can carry out the daily tasks. The following seven phases should be followed in approximately this order. Within these sections, you will find relevant online courses to get you started, as well as key things to focus on in each phase. Phase 1: Programming – Excel, SQL, Python/R Programming requirements

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: for data analysts can vary widely across fields and positions. However, most data analyst positions can be fulfilled with knowledge of Excel, SQL, and some simple Python or R. While Excel may seem old school, it’s still a much-used and very valuable tool that is easy to learn and produces quick results that explain the current state of the data. Excel is mostly used for analyzing the data to determine summaries and trends. SQL is used to retrieve data for analysis from databases that can then be

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: worked on using Excel or a programming language. Python and R are, essentially, the two go-to data analysis programming languages, with Python being more popular than R due to its ease of use. Online courses you can take to learn programming skills: Below is a selection of courses that can be used to quickly learn the fundamentals of the programming required for data analysis. By no means is this an extensive list or the only resources out there for learning how to code, but these resources give

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: a good starting point. Remember, this is a roadmap to get you the basic skills necessary to be able to fulfill a data analyst position and carry out their daily tasks, therefore breadth of programming knowledge is the goal here, not depth. It’s also important to note that most data analysts pick between Python or R and make that their primary programming language. Make your decision based on that which is used most predominantly in your target industry. End of phase objectives: At the end of

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: this phase, you should be able to write code that runs in your chosen target languages. Extensive knowledge of each language is unnecessary except for the parts that are necessary to conduct an analysis. It’s important to note that programming is a task best learned through doing. You can sit and watch these videos and claim to know how to code by the end of them, but there is a distinct difference between watching and doing. Therefore, it’s advised to work along with the videos and then

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: practice writing your own code afterward to see if you can still make it work. Further practice in writing code will occur in later phases. Phase 2: Mathematics – Arithmetic, Algebra, Statistics, and Probability If you completed high school/secondary school, or the first couple of years of college or university courses, you will have generally learned all of the mathematics you need to know to become a data analyst (field and position-dependent). Cool, right? Unlike data science where you need

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: to have a deep understanding of linear algebra, calculus, and further mathematical disciplines which can take years to master, most data analyst positions will require just the basic mathematics that you learned early on in your education. Therefore, this phase should just be a review of what you have already learned and possibly knocking the cobwebs off your statistics and probability knowledge. The courses below are from Khan Academy, a favorite for learning math through bite-sized, easily

content: digestible lessons that explain concepts in simple terms for individuals at any level. title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: company is paying its staff on average. Alternatively, you need to be able to determine who the outliers are in an age group of people who subscribe to a website newsletter. Or, you need to be able to calculate unknown values in a data set that is looking to determine the velocity of sparrows but only gives the distance and time of their flight. The mathematical skills developed in this phase will be practiced and enhanced in later phases. Phase 3: Data Analysis – Collecting, Cleaning, Analyzing

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: Data analysis is the meat and potatoes of what a data analyst does. Data analysis can be broken down into five steps that are universally recognized. Determine the driving question: Recognizing the driving question or overall objective of the data analysis helps set the stage for what data you need and what the result of the analysis should reveal. Data collection: Defining the data you need to answer your driving question will help you collect the right data for the job. At the end of the day,

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: it’s better to have more data that gives a clear picture of what you’re looking for than too little data. Data cleaning: It’s time to turn the raw data you’ve collected into something you can analyze through the data cleaning process. This involves amending or removing incorrect or irrelevant data, checking for data completeness, removing duplicates, or producing important values, such as means or averages. Data analysis: Analyzing the data you’ve cleaned involves looking for insights within the

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: data, including patterns, relationships, and the possibility for predictions. Interpretation: This phase involves producing visualizations of the results of your data analysis. These visualizations will tell the story of your data and will answer the question in a manner that’s easy to comprehend and straight to the point. Resources to help you learn the data analysis process: End of phase objectives: By the end of this phase, you should be able to conduct a full data analysis following the

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: steps listed above using the programming and mathematical skills learned previously. Complete fluency in these stages is not required yet as there will be a phase later on where portfolio projects will be created that will enhance the skills learned here. Phase 4: Data Visualization While data visualization is taught as part of the five steps of data analysis, it gets its own special phase here because it plays such a large part in the daily tasks of data analysts. Being able to create

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: compelling, accurate visualizations is one of the fundamental cornerstones of this career, therefore special attention should be paid to these skills. Tableau is one of the most common tools used by data analysts to create visualizations, and resources to learn it will be included below. Other data visualization tools include QlikView, Microsoft Power BI, Datawrapper, Plotly, and more that may be relevant depending on your target field or position. This roadmap will focus on one of the most

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: prominent, Tableau. Resources to help get you started with Tableau: End of phase objectives: By the end of this phase, you should be able to create data visualizations that accurately represent the findings of your data analysis. These visualizations must be eye-catching, easy to understand, and must provide a clear picture of the results without skewing the information visually. Phase 5: Industry Knowledge Industry knowledge is the industry-specific tool you will use to solve problems daily.

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: For example, a background in forestry practices and forest management is important if you are to be conducting data analyses on how many trees should be cut each year to ensure a healthy forest grows. Alternatively, you need to have the business acumen to be able to determine if a company is in trouble financially based on the results of your analysis. Furthermore, if you were to work as an analyst for a hospital that is seeking to find the most efficient way to schedule staff during busy

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: periods, it’s important to have an understanding of the important roles that each person plays in a hospital. Essentially, you have the skills to conduct data analyses, but now you need to gain the skills and knowledge to be able to apply them to a specific industry. Whether you’re entering a completely different industry or are wanting to return to your current industry as an analyst, it never hurts to brush up on industry knowledge. Studying the latest can help keep you relevant as an analyst

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: who can identify trends, see patterns, and improve the efficiency and effectiveness of those around them. Gaining industry knowledge can be done by reading journal articles, attending lectures at universities, listening to podcasts, reading newsletters, talking to people in the industry, and more. End of phase objectives: By the end of this phase, you want to be able to conduct analyses that are relevant and provide insightful conclusions to problems in your target industry. For those looking to

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: work in business, this means conducting analyses to determine the cost-benefit structure of a company decision. For those looking to work in the sciences, this means being able to disseminate conclusions from piles of evidence that may or may not support a hypothesis. For those looking to work in healthcare, this means being able to conduct analyses that provide insight into the working conditions required to maintain a happy staff. The point is that you need to be comfortable analyzing the data

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: of a particular industry and be able to provide conclusions to the problems you are trying to solve. Phase 6: Portfolio Building your personal portfolio is the fun part of this roadmap. Here, you get the chance to build personal data analysis projects that showcase your skills and prove to employers that they want you on their team. These projects should include all of the skills you’ve learned thus far and should be relevant to your target industry. This means that they use the tools of the

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: industry, draw meaningful conclusions, and perhaps even add to the knowledge base of the industry. These projects can be unique, can be inspired by those seen on the internet, or can include pro bono work done for a small company in your area. A quick browse of the internet can give you a bunch of ideas and datasets you can use to create your own projects. Not only that, but portfolios give you the chance to put all of

title: The Complete Roadmap to Becoming a Data Analyst With No Previous Experience
content: your skills together to produce projects that yield results. Phase 7: Networking, Job Applications, and Technical Interview Prep The final phase of our roadmap brings us to networking, job applications, and technical interview prep. You have the skills. Networking will involve attending conferences and industry events, talking to recruiters, and rubbing elbows with people who are currently analysts who may be

Job applications will come next, followed by preparing for technical interviews. title: The 3 Pillars of Math You Need to Know to Become an Effective Data Analyst
content: The amount of math you are told you should know and the amount of math you will use daily as a data analyst, are two very different things. Field (and sometimes project) dependent, there are only a few small subsections of mathematics that most data analysts use daily. While most educational programs discuss the big three math topics all data analysts should know (linear algebra, statistics, and calculus), not all fields or positions require in-depth knowledge of calculus or advanced topics.

title: The 3 Pillars of Math You Need to Know to Become an Effective Data Analyst
content: While learning the more advanced topics in math (such as calculus and beyond) adds valuable tools to your arsenal and teaches you how to problem solve, it can also be a sticking point that may stop you from advancing in your path towards becoming a data analyst. Therefore, unless your target field or position requires advanced mathematical knowledge and training, it can be beneficial to focus on the essential parts that can fulfill 70% or more of the daily requirements of most data analyst

content: positions. Luckily, you will likely have already studied the three pillars discussed in this article if you have completed a few years of university courses or took advanced math courses in high school or secondary school. 1. Linear Algebra Linear algebra is the branch of mathematics dedicated to solving linear equations for unknown values and is also the foundation upon which knowledge of machine learning is built. While machine learning may be outside the scope of what a general data analyst

title: The 3 Pillars of Math You Need to Know to Become an Effective Data Analyst
content: will do daily, the fundamental concepts of linear algebra will be used during data preprocessing and data transformation. Additionally, linear algebra teaches you to think logically through a progression of steps which is beneficial when working through an analysis that focuses on answering a particular question or solving a specific problem. Concepts in linear algebra include vectors and spaces, matrix transformations, and alternate coordinate systems. Vectors can be used in Data Analysis to

title: The 3 Pillars of Math You Need to Know to Become an Effective Data Analyst
content: calculate how different a prediction from a data set is from an expected output after data transformation. Matrix transformations are used to transform one vector into another vector which allows for data to be represented geometrically in a two- or three-dimensional space during data transformation. Alternate coordinate systems can be used in data analysis to change how datasets are represented visually to ensure that data is appropriately represented. Resources to learn linear algebra Linear

title: The 3 Pillars of Math You Need to Know to Become an Effective Data Analyst
content: Algebra | Khan Academy How to use linear algebra for data analysis Linear Algebra Essentials with Numpy (part 1) 2. Probability Probability is the study of how likely something is to happen and is essential for drawing conclusions that can help decision-making during uncertain situations. While probability and statistics are linked and are often lumped together for study, the two are used to determine different conclusions. Probability has many practical uses in all fields, such as determining

title: The 3 Pillars of Math You Need to Know to Become an Effective Data Analyst
content: the likelihood that a recession will occur, the likelihood that a disease is tied to the frequency of a gene, or even the likelihood that a visitor to a website will subscribe to its newsletter. Two types of probability exist that can be used to look at data sets. Classical probability is the type of probability that involves a set of rules attached to it. For example, you could have a rule that the probability of a customer purchasing from a website must be greater than 0.33 for it to be valid.

title: The 3 Pillars of Math You Need to Know to Become an Effective Data Analyst
content: Relative frequency is the type of probability looking at the occurrence ratio of a single event in relation to the total number of possible outcomes. For example, this could be used to compare the result of a subset of data to the total amount of collected data. Resources to learn probability How to use probability for data analysis 3. Statistics Statistics is the branch of Mathematics surrounding data collection, analysis, presentation, and interpretation. Statistics and probability are linked

title: The 3 Pillars of Math You Need to Know to Become an Effective Data Analyst
content: and often taught together, though they yield different answers to different questions. Statistics are the meat and potatoes of data analysis and provide the fundamentals for understanding what data sets tell us. Statistics can be divided into two types: descriptive and inferential. Descriptive statistics describe the characteristics of a population and can be further subdivided into measures of central tendency and measures of variability which measure different aspects of a population. For

title: The 3 Pillars of Math You Need to Know to Become an Effective Data Analyst
content: example, descriptive statistics can be used to conclude a range of test scores collected or the mean age of people who sign up for a website newsletter. Inferential statistics make predictions about a population based on sample data. For example, hypothesis testing, a type of inferential statistics, can be used to determine whether or not a hypothesis about a population can be accepted or rejected based on a study sample. Probability and statistics are the backbone of data analysis and will allow you to complete more than 70% of the daily requirements of a data analyst (position and industry dependent). Becoming a data

While this article covers the fundamentals of mathematics that support most daily data analyst work, it’s not to say that your learning of math should stop there. Data analysts remain relevant and advance in their careers by continuing to learn. This means expanding your knowledge beyond the fundamentals and

title: The 3 Pillars of Math You Need to Know to Become an Effective Data Analyst
content: taking deeper dives into more complex mathematics that, as mentioned above, will give you more tools in your arsenal and will fine-tune your problem-solving skills. Mathematics is the way of understanding what data is telling us and helps us draw conclusions that allow us to make decisions moving forward. By furthering your knowledge you give yourself the ability to look at data sets and results from different standpoints and to resolve problems in different ways. Therefore, don’t stop at the

title: How to ace Technical Interviews(Excel) for Business Intelligence Engineer/Data Analyst at FAANG
content: Excel is one of the most versatile tools when it comes to data. You can do all things data in Excel, starting from data entry to data manipulation to data analysis to data reporting to data automation. Photo by Mika Baumeister on Unsplash No wonder it features as a pre-requisite to Data Analyst roles at almost all IT companies, no matter the sector. Here are the top-five excel formulas to prepare if you are appearing for a data analyst interview at FAANG (or any company). 1. COUNTIF COUNTIF is

title: How to ace Technical Interviews(Excel) for Business Intelligence Engineer/Data Analyst at FAANG
content: an advanced IF function and applies criteria to cells across multiple ranges and counts the number of times all criteria are met. Take, for instance, one of the questions I was asked in the Excel Interview at Amazon was on Pareto’s principle. As per wikipedia.com – The Pareto principle states that for many outcomes, roughly 80% of consequences come from 20% of causes (the "vital few"). I was given a data set** with the sales by product category and product ID. My task was to find out the set of

title: How to ace Technical Interviews(Excel) for Business Intelligence Engineer/Data Analyst at FAANG
content: product IDs contributing to 80% of Sales. Image by Author Solution – There are multiple ways, this can be solved. In order to solve it, we need to count the number of top-selling products which contribute to 80% of the total sales. I used a combination of COUNTIF and SUM formulas. Here’s what I did – Find out the sum of all sales by _totalsales= SUM(C1:C600) Find out 80% of total sales by _Sales_80= 0.8*totalsales Sort the data set by sales in descending order. Calculate the cumulative Sales at

title: How to ace Technical Interviews(Excel) for Business Intelligence Engineer/Data Analyst at FAANG
content: each row by – _cumsales(Column D)=SUM($C$1:C2) Find out the number of product IDs where the cum_sales are greater than Sales_80(H5) by the following formula COUNTIF(D1:D600,"<=" &$H$5) The result will give the count of Top-Selling product IDs which are contributing to 80% of sales. There was another dataset and three more questions that could be solved just by using the COUNTIF function. 2. DATEDIF For some reason, DATEDIF is not a listed function in Excel. What I mean by listed is that you will

title: How to ace Technical Interviews(Excel) for Business Intelligence Engineer/Data Analyst at FAANG
content: not get any suggestions when you type it. But it is supported nevertheless. DATEDIF function lets you subtract two dates and outputs the result in specified time-frequency like – days, months, years, etc. a. A question asked in the Interview at Amazon consisted of a data set** on students with attributes such as the birth date and class section. My task was to find the age of students who were born after 10 March 2003 and were in section A. Solution – As always, there are multiple ways a problem

title: How to ace Technical Interviews(Excel) for Business Intelligence Engineer/Data Analyst at FAANG
content: can be solved. I used DATEDIF function to calculate the age and used multiple IF formulae to filter the students from section A and born after 10 March 2003. The final formula looked like this – =IF(section="A", If (dob>DATE(2003,3,10), DATEDIF(dob,today(),"y")," ")," ") Knowing these functions really simplifies the task to just one line instead of calculating multiple intermediate columns. b. Another question on the same data set was to calculate the number of students from Section A born

title: How to ace Technical Interviews(Excel) for Business Intelligence Engineer/Data Analyst at FAANG
content: before 3 April 2002 with ages more than 12 years. Solution – I solved it in two steps. First I marked the students who satisfied this criterion with 1 and others as 0. Then, I took SUM of the column to get the number of students who satisfied the asked criteria. This could further be simplified but at the time, this was what came to my mind. Col F= IF(B1="A",IF(C1<DATE(2002,4,3), IF(DATEDIF(C1,today(),"y") >12,1,0),0) = SUM(Col F) Simplified Version using COUNTIFS(Similar to CountIF but you can

title: How to ace Technical Interviews(Excel) for Business Intelligence Engineer/Data Analyst at FAANG
content: specify more than one condition) =COUNTIFS(B1:B60,"A", C1:C60, "<"&DATE(2002,4,3),E1:E60,">"&12) Column B = Section, Column C = Date of Birth, Column E = Age (Calculated as DATEDIF(C1,today(),"y")) There was another dataset. Three questions followed to answer on which option was the best for a company. All these questions could be solved easily using datedif and Sum functions. 3. INDEX/MATCH INDEX returns the value at a given location in a range or array. MATCH function returns the index of the

title: How to ace Technical Interviews(Excel) for Business Intelligence Engineer/Data Analyst at FAANG
content: cell which satisfies the specified condition in a given range. Together both these functions can help find an exact match or a value that is greater or lesser than the lookup value. This combination is similar to VLOOKUP. But there are a few drawbacks to using VLOOKUP. First is that it assumes by default that the first column in the table array is sorted alphabetically. The second is, you can’t look up the value in any column other than the first column using VLOOKUP. A dataset** from the

title: How to ace Technical Interviews(Excel) for Business Intelligence Engineer/Data Analyst at FAANG
content: interview at Amazon was about Sales and Profits per region. There were two questions on this dataset. Image by Author a. First was to find the name of the region with a specified sales amount. Solution – I tried using VLOOKUP here and when it didn’t work, I realized the limitations of VLOOKUP. So, I switched to INDEX MATCH instead. It was a simple formula that gave me the correct answer as South— =INDEX(A2:A9,MATCH(13440,B2:B9,0)) b. The Second question was to find the region with the lowest

title: How to ace Technical Interviews(Excel) for Business Intelligence Engineer/Data Analyst at FAANG
content: Profits. Solution – I used the same formula here. Just changed the sales value with the minimum profit and I got the correct answer again. =INDEX(A2:A9,MATCH(MIN(C2:C9),C2:C9,0)) 4. SUMPRODUCT According to support.microsoft.com, SUMPRODUCT function returns the sum of the products of corresponding ranges or arrays. The default operation is multiplication, but addition, subtraction, and division are also possible. Although I have not used this formula very often, it was used in one of the

title: How to ace Technical Interviews(Excel) for Business Intelligence Engineer/Data Analyst at FAANG
content: questions asked in this interview. In this dataset**, Employees and their dates of joining were given. The task was to find out how many employees joined in the months of January, February, March, and so on. Solution – Again, there are multiple ways to do this, and I did not use SUMPRODUCT in the interview. But it is the most straightforward if SUMPRODUCT is used. The formula can be written like this – =SUMPRODUCT((MONTH(B$7:B$81) = 1)*(B$7:B$81<>"")) We are getting the array where the month of

title: How to ace Technical Interviews(Excel) for Business Intelligence Engineer/Data Analyst at FAANG
content: dates of joining (Column B) is equal to 1 (for January) and then multiplying it by another array to handle null values. A little more details on the second part here – The MONTH Function returns 1 if you pass an empty value to this function. This will be counted in the month of January which is inaccurate. So, we create an array/range indicating non-null values and mark 1 for non-null and 0 for null. This takes care of the empty values as well as gives us an array to use for the SUMPRODUCT

title: How to ace Technical Interviews(Excel) for Business Intelligence Engineer/Data Analyst at FAANG
content: function. 5. SUMIF SUMIF function returns the sum of the values in a range that meet the specified criteria. Even though there were no questions asked in the interviews which were directly based on this formula, this is a simple and frequently used function that can help answer questions where you need to sum selectively. Like, in the data set** on students with attributes such as the birth date and class section, you could be asked to find the total projects completed by students in Section A.

title: How to ace Technical Interviews(Excel) for Business Intelligence Engineer/Data Analyst at FAANG
content: SUMIF could be used to find that answer easily. These were the five excel functions I find very useful and use frequently as a data analyst. I hope you find this information useful and wish you the best of luck for your upcoming interviews/preparation. Bonus Tip: Try to solve a problem by applying these functions. Sometimes, we have read about the functions and feel confident about the usage. But we can’t recall them at the time of interviews(personal experience). Taking a dataset and solving

title: How to ace Technical Interviews(Excel) for Business Intelligence Engineer/Data Analyst at FAANG
content: few questions using these functions really helps in combining multiple functions and understanding the scenarios where they can be applied. Thanks for reading! Until next time… *All data sets have been completely changed keeping the interview concept same. No data has been released from the actual interview. The solutions provided are my own.

title: GitHub Analytical Workflow for Data Analysts
content: Hello world! I’m writing my very first article on Medium and decided to share how I introduced GitHub to my data team to promote collaboration. I’ll talk about why having GitHub can help a team (more than 2 data folks) collaborate more effectively, and how you can implement GitHub into your day-to-day data analytical workflows. This should help set you up for establishing some form of collaborative framework within your team. In this article, I will focus on the following topics: Table of

title: GitHub Analytical Workflow for Data Analysts
content: Contents: Why GitHub What you need before starting Branching Strategy What else you can add Why GitHub If you’re working in the data space and have worked with at least one other teammate, chances are you have encountered collaborative issues like working on the latest code version, tracking who has edited what code or frustratingly trying to recall what purpose was this code written for which was last edited XX days ago. These are just some of the pain points that I have heard from fellow data

title: GitHub Analytical Workflow for Data Analysts
content: folks and my personal experience. Though I suspect all of these are merely scratching the tip of the iceberg. So how exactly can GitHub tackle these? With GitHub, analysts can utilise its Version Control System (VCS) and Git to work on the same data project together. Any changes made to the project can be updated, tracked and reviewed by fellow analysts, and any earlier versions of the work can also be recovered. While GitHub is most popularly used with software development, we can take a leaf

title: GitHub Analytical Workflow for Data Analysts
content: out of the book and incorporate some of it into data analytical workflows. What you need before starting Before introducing GitHub to your team, it’s important to first understand the basics of GitHub. Knowing how to add, commit, push files and create pull requests. I will not be going into these basics as there are plenty of resources and articles out there already that provides a comprehensive guide on mastering these basics. Here are some useful quick links: Introduction to Github for Data

title: GitHub Analytical Workflow for Data Analysts
content: Scientists Once you have a basic grasp on how git works, the next thing to decide is what type of branching strategy to employ for your team. Branching Strategy and Directories What exactly is a branching strategy? It’s essentially a strategy used typically by software developers to write, merge, and ship code in the context of a VCS like Git. Choosing a suitable model is important to determine when and how changes are made and committed back to the codebase. 4 branching workflows for Git

title: GitHub Analytical Workflow for Data Analysts
content: Personal BranchesThe simplest form of branching strategy is to have the main branch serve as the main source of the codebase, and have each team member create a branch off mainwith their name as the branch name (i.e. person-A, person-B etc.). All of the personal branches will merge into main. This works when the team is small (< 3), and there are few complexities in terms of the work involved (i.e. frequency of new projects is low). As the projects scale up, this approach may be insufficient to

title: GitHub Analytical Workflow for Data Analysts
content: handle the various commits and could lead to confusion. Here’s a snippet on how it looks like. First, create a new repository: ## git template for creating a new repository on the command line echo "# playground" >> README.md git init git add README.md git commit -m "first commit" git branch -M main git remote add origin <git url> git push -u origin main Now that you have a main branch that tracks remote branch ‘main’ from ‘origin’, you and your team can create new branches from main. # new

title: GitHub Analytical Workflow for Data Analysts
content: branches for each teammate git checkout -b "person-A" git checkout -b "person-B" git branch BAM. Now you have two branches for each user to work on their projects separately to be pushed to main once their part or the entirety of the project is completed. Project-based BranchingA more efficient yet lightweight approach is to adopt a project-based branching model, which is essentially a simplified model of Git Flow. The main branch serves as the main source of codebase, and project branches are

title: GitHub Analytical Workflow for Data Analysts
content: used to develop new projects to be merged into main. git checkout -b 'project-A' git checkout -b 'project-B' git branch If there is more than one user working on the same project, more downstream branches can be created from the main project branch. E.g. project-A/person-A, project-A/person-B. Double BAM. How it worksLet’s take a look at how a change can be incorporated for a team member, Dave, working on project titled "analytics101" using project-based branching as an example. These are some

title: GitHub Analytical Workflow for Data Analysts
content: of the branches that will exist: main analytics101 analytics101/dave (present only if there are more than 1 person working on the same project) etc. Once Dave has completed a part or the project itself within the branch analytics101, he wishes to commit all the changes to the main branch for anyone else to reference from. git add -A # staging all the changes git commit -m "Commit for Project A" git push He can then proceed to create a Pull Request for this commit to be merged to the main branch.

title: GitHub Analytical Workflow for Data Analysts
content: Directory StructureIt is important to note that branching is not the same as directory. The directories within your git repository should be set up in a way that make sense for the team, similarly to how files are stored in different categories of folders and with various levels, either locally or on a shared enterprise cloud. However, I do recommend having a folder each for a new project to not complicate things, with each folder having a README.md to describe the project folder. What else you

title: GitHub Analytical Workflow for Data Analysts
content: can add Once you have GitHub and a branching strategy in place, you can add on more tools that can help the team to collaborate further! EnvironmentsA common programming tool that Data analysts use is python, an object-oriented language that is efficient in data wrangling, visualisation and machine learning etc. Most analysts will interact with python via Jupyter Notebook, either on the Conda environment itself or through IDEs such as Visual Studio Code. An issue with using python and notebooks

title: GitHub Analytical Workflow for Data Analysts
content: when collaborating with numerous teammates is the risk of dependencies breaking apart as a result of different versions used. This is where environments and git come in handy. For each of the new projects, simply initiate and activate a new environment and store all the dependencies into a file (requirements.txt). Anyone can simply access the project subdirectory, activate a new environment and install the required dependencies to run the code successfully. Inserting Credentials If you find

title: GitHub Analytical Workflow for Data Analysts
content: yourself having to query data into your local machine, one issue you might face is having to manually insert your credentials into an engine. While there are numerous methods to circumvent this, an example would be to leverage on environment variables via python-dotenv package. Using this method together with Git becomes handy as you can simply add the .envfile to a .gitignore and the file containing all your credentials will be safely stored only on your local machine. Storing credentials the

title: GitHub Analytical Workflow for Data Analysts
content: right way! Once you have your credentials stored on a .env file, you can load the variables. # load env variables  import os %load_ext dotenv  %dotenv USERNAME = os.getenv("USERNAME")  PASSWORD = os.getenv("PASSWORD") Now that you have your credentials loaded as variables, you can simply insert them to your SQL engine to extract the relevant data. Triple BAM. Hopefully with all of these, anyone can get started with Git and incorporating them into their data analytical workflows. Please leave

title: GitHub Analytical Workflow for Data Analysts
content: comments 💬 if there’s more to add and I will be happy to include them in an edit! Thanks for reading! 🙂

title: Data Scientist vs Data Analyst vs Data Engineer
content: Data is the new oil. Data scientist, the sexiest job of the 21st century. Without data analytics, companies are blind and deaf. …… Data science has become one of the hottest professions in recent years. High demand in the market, lucrative compensation, fat cheque, and sexy job title all make new graduates or ones who are looking for a career change keen to get into this area. However, the job titles and the work allocation in a data team could be confusing. "I like to play around with data",

title: Data Scientist vs Data Analyst vs Data Engineer
content: "I’m a data-driven person" are not enough to find the most suitable career for you in the data field. The worst scenario could be wasting loads of time on applying for jobs you’re not suitable for at all or landing a job that you thought you were interested in but actually not and ending up losing passion. It took me some time to really understand the differences between each role in a data team. There were 2 mistakes I made when I first applied for jobs in this area. The first one is I applied

title: Data Scientist vs Data Analyst vs Data Engineer
content: for all jobs that have ‘data’ in the title, simply because I didn’t know the differences and thought "I’ll get into this area first and everything will sort out itself". Data engineer, data architect, business analyst, Data Analyst, data scientist, business intelligence analyst, data master, data guru, you name it. As long as the role has something to do with data it’s on my application list. It was time-consuming, extremely inefficient, and very goalless. The second mistake is not knowing what

title: Data Scientist vs Data Analyst vs Data Engineer
content: I really want to do about data. Initially, I thought I was so going to be a data scientist cause I like data and it’s the sexiest title. After started working on actual projects, I realised that what I really enjoyed was analysing data, finding out insight, and contributing to business decisions, which are more of a data analyst. This story aims to help you understand what each of the 3 roles does in a data team, and therefore hopefully help you find out what really excites you. To illustrate

title: Data Scientist vs Data Analyst vs Data Engineer
content: what each role does in a team, we first need to understand the journey of data from being generated to being presented in front of business decision makers. Let’s use an e-commerce website as an example and go through the journey of data from a 30000-foot view. A Journey of Data When you go onto a website and browse over the merchandise, all of your behaviours are tracked and monitored. What products you browsed, how you hovered your mouse across the page, how long you stayed on the website,

title: Data Scientist vs Data Analyst vs Data Engineer
content: what your user journey was, what you purchased, how much you spent, etc. This information (data) is recorded and sent to a place, usually a cloud. It could be hosted by a provider like AWS, Azure, GCP, etc, or on-premise servers. Image by Author At this stage, the data is often stored in a very raw form, maybe even not structured. To make these data available to be queried, we need to move them to a database. There are many kinds of databases with different characteristics, usages, and

title: Data Scientist vs Data Analyst vs Data Engineer
content: capabilities to choose from based on your demands. Data cleaning and transformation would happen at this stage too. For example, turning data structure into tabular format, flattening data that is in JSON, aggregation based on business logic, data validation, etc. This process is what we called ETL, extract (from the cloud), transform (the data), load (into a database). (The modern infrastructure favours ELT, i.e transforming the data after loading them into a database. We will cover that in

title: Data Scientist vs Data Analyst vs Data Engineer
content: another story.) The purpose of this stage is to provide data consumers with a collection of clean, validated, and usable data. Image by Author Now the usable data is sitting in the database. There are 2 main things we can do about it. Either analyse the data and find insights to make business decisions or use the data as materials to build some fascinating products like machine learning, deep learning, NLP, recommendation system, etc. Image by Author Remits of each role Data Analyst Data

title: Data Scientist vs Data Analyst vs Data Engineer
content: analysts are one of the data consumers. A data analyst answers questions about the present such as: what is going on now? What are the causes? Can you show me XYZ? What should we do to avoid/achieve ABC? What is the trend in the past 3 years? Is our product doing well? Let’s re-think what is data. Data is something that has already taken place. A data-driven decision means we look at what has already happened, interpret the insight of it, and then make our next step based on that. A data

title: Data Scientist vs Data Analyst vs Data Engineer
content: analyst’s job includes 3 main parts: Understand the metrics/business problem, i.e ask the right questions. Find out the answers or more insights from the data. Communication. This includes creating dashboards with appropriate visualisations and explaining them in an easy-understanding way to non-tech stakeholders. Skills requirements SQL: This is essential for all data-related roles to interact with databases. Data visualisation: The more important thing is knowing how to visualise the data in a

title: Data Scientist vs Data Analyst vs Data Engineer
content: proper way, rather than the tool you use. Most companies have licensed Business Intelligence tools like Power BI, Tableau, Looker, Qlik, etc. You don’t need to know how to use all of them. If you understand the core concepts of data analysis, it shouldn’t take you long to pick up any one of them. Domain knowledge: I’d say domain knowledge is much more critical for a data analyst than other roles. What are the metrics stand for? How do metrics interact with each other? What are the needle movers?

title: Data Scientist vs Data Analyst vs Data Engineer
content: These kinds of domain knowledge are necessary to ask the right questions, to be able to find out insights and to contribute to business decisions. Data Scientist Data scientists are another data consumer. Instead of answering questions about the present, they try to find patterns in the data and answer the questions about the future, i.e prediction. This technique **** has actually existed for a long time. You must have heard of it, it’s called _statistic_s. Machine learning and deep learning

title: Data Scientist vs Data Analyst vs Data Engineer
content: are the 2 most popular ways to utilise the power of computers to find patterns in data. Data scientists also build products based on those predictions. For instance, a recommendation system predicts what you like, a ranking system predicts the order of popularity, NLP predicts what a sentence means. Data scientists build these products not to help make business decisions, but to solve business problems. The best way to describe a data scientist is someone who "use data to solve the company’s

title: Data Scientist vs Data Analyst vs Data Engineer
content: problems". This could be anything, depending on the company’s size. You might see a data scientist doing lots of analyst’s and engineer’s jobs in a small startup. In a larger company, they are more likely to focus on what we just talked about. Skills requirements: SQL: This is essential for all data-related roles to interact with databases. Statistics/Mathematics: You have to master statistics knowledge such as theories behind each machine learning method, probabilities, etc to solve more

title: Data Scientist vs Data Analyst vs Data Engineer
content: complex problems. This part is quite academic and theoretical, that’s why most of the data scientist roles would require a Master or PhD degree. Programming skills: To apply statistics knowledge to solve real-world problems, you have to equip yourself with programming skills. Training models, writing algorithms, building next-generation products are all done on a laptop. Data science is a subject that combines computer science and statistics. Currently, Python and R are the most popular

title: Data Scientist vs Data Analyst vs Data Engineer
content: programming language. Software development: Just like any other engineer, software development skills are essential to cooperate with other stakeholders. Git workflow, CI/CD, DevOps, etc are all basic in a data scientist’s arsenal. Data Engineer How do data analysts and scientists get the data? How does the data come from user behaviour to the database? How do we make sure the data is accountable? The answer is data engineers. Data consumers cannot perform their work without having data

title: Data Scientist vs Data Analyst vs Data Engineer
content: engineers set up the whole structure. They build data pipelines to ingest data from users’ devices to the cloud then to the database. To put it in a simple way, everything that happens to the data before reaching the database is taken care of by data engineers. A data engineer cares most about: How to ingest data from disparate sources to one single destination for analysts and scientists to consume. Make sure the data pipeline, storage, data structure are optimised and most cost-efficient for

title: Data Scientist vs Data Analyst vs Data Engineer
content: the company. Make sure the data that analysts and scientists use is the most updated, validated and accountable. They won’t make wrong decisions because the data is incorrect. Skills requirements SQL: In addition, a data engineer should understand the ins and outs of each different database, when to use which, what are their edges. Sometimes need to know DBA (database administration) commands like monitoring accesses of team members, writing procedures, maintaining schemas to optimise database

title: Data Scientist vs Data Analyst vs Data Engineer
content: performance. Cloud computing: As now nearly all of the data is on the cloud, from storage to database to warehousing, engineers have to be very familiar with the cloud computing technology. AWS (Amazon), Azure (Microsoft), and GCP (Google) are the 3 most popular cloud services in the market. This also includes the application of parallel computing (Hadoop, Spark) and big data. Software development: Same as the abovementioned. Summary To use one sentence to summarise each role, Business decisions

title: Data Scientist vs Data Analyst vs Data Engineer
content: are driven by data analysts. Data scientists solve business problems. Data engineers enable data analysts and scientists to perform their work. Image by Author Although the real situation varies in different companies depending on the size and organisation structure, the main purposes of each role shouldn’t be too far off from what we just discussed. It’s unlikely to see a data analyst playing around with AWS and setting up data pipelines and a data engineer building up dashboards in Looker. A

title: Data Scientist vs Data Analyst vs Data Engineer
content: data scientist, though, could be doing anything. In his video, Joma explains how the organisation would look like in different scales of companies pretty well. He also gives a pretty clear walk-through of Data Science history and what really is data science. Finally, the best thing I would highly recommend to do is instead of just looking at the titles, looking closely at the job description, to really understand what this role does in their company and if those day to day works meet your

title: Data Scientist vs Data Analyst vs Data Engineer

title: How I Landed a Data Analyst Job in 4 Months
content: At the height of the pandemic, I landed my first data analyst job. As a fresh graduate with little experience, it was definitely challenging. But after four months of applying, interviewing, and preparing, I received multiple job offers. In this article, I’ll explain what you can expect in these interviews and how you can best prepare to land your first data analyst job. Technical Assessment (SQL, R, Python) Image by Caspar Camille Rubin on Unsplash Most data analyst interviews include a

title: How I Landed a Data Analyst Job in 4 Months
content: technical assessment to test your coding abilities in relevant languages such as SQL, Python, or R. The assessment is done either live – working on a problem in front of your interviewer – or through a take-home assignment. I’ve experienced more live interviews which is a different experience from assignments (more on this later). SQL In most data analyst roles, SQL skills are a must as you need it to retrieve data from a database. If you cannot pull your data, then you cannot do your job – no

title: How I Landed a Data Analyst Job in 4 Months
content: data, no analysis. I was given a SQL assessment for nearly every company I interviewed with, which typically came after the initial screening. **** So, how exactly did I prepare for the SQL assessment? For me, solving SQL practice questions was the most useful. HackerRank and Leetcode are great resources. The easy level questions on HackerRank are great for learning the basics (i.e. joining, aggregating, filtering, etc.). Leetcode questions are a bit more involved. I found that once I was able

title: How I Landed a Data Analyst Job in 4 Months
content: to solve the easy level questions on Leetcode consistently (aim to solve them within 15 minutes), I had no trouble with the SQL assessments. I would recommend to think out loud while you are working on these questions as this is expected during a live coding interview. A lot of times, interviewers are more interested in how you articulate your thought process rather than you arriving at the perfect solution. Furthermore, if you communicate clearly, interviewers will often provide hints or nudge

title: How I Landed a Data Analyst Job in 4 Months
content: you in the right direction if you are stuck. In addition to helping me pass SQL assessments, putting the time into solving these challenges has been invaluable for me in my current data analyst role. While the context of Leetcode questions is different from what I face at my job, the techniques I learned from solving these problems have been applicable in the workplace. Python/R Although none of my technical assessments included Python or R, I prepared a lot for them as these tools are necessary

title: How I Landed a Data Analyst Job in 4 Months
content: for any data analyst. I like the site Datacamp due to its gamified approach to learning. While sites like Datacamp helped me to learn basic concepts, I only felt comfortable with my coding abilities after working on projects as it allowed me to apply these concepts in a real-world environment. This is one reason why it’s important to work on projects if you are new to the field (see next section). Build a Portfolio Image from Author’s Portfolio For those with little to no experience, building a

title: How I Landed a Data Analyst Job in 4 Months
content: portfolio is imperative. One benefit of having a portfolio of relevant projects is that it makes your resume stand out. Because data analytics is a popular field, you are competing against a large pool of candidates. If you are new to the field, many candidates will have more experience than you, so building a portfolio is one way to make your application more competitive. In fact, one company actually reached out to me because they were impressed with my portfolio and wanted to discuss my

title: How I Landed a Data Analyst Job in 4 Months
content: projects. Another benefit of having a portfolio is that it gives you more ammunition during an interview. As a fresh graduate, I had little professional experience, so having a portfolio gave me more to talk about during interviews. It also proved that I was capable of solving problems despite my lack of work experience. What kind of project should you work on? I would recommend working on something original. By original, I mean a project in which you define your own problem, pull your own data,

title: How I Landed a Data Analyst Job in 4 Months
content: clean the data, then analyze that data – analyzing Kaggle’s Titanic dataset won’t make you stand out. An original project will not only signal that you are capable of solving analytical problems, but it will show that you are interested in the field and highly motivated. I’ve linked my portfolio as an example. Furthermore, this article can help you to develop project ideas. Have an In-Depth Knowledge of Your Projects Image by airfocus on Unsplash Be prepared to talk about your projects in

title: How I Landed a Data Analyst Job in 4 Months
content: detail. In every interview, I was asked to talk about a project I worked on. Most times, the interviewer let me choose the project. In these cases, I chose the project that I was the most proud of. Give a high-level overview of your project first (motivation, goal, method, result, etc.). The interviewer will ask follow up questions (where you got your data, the biggest challenges you faced, etc.), so be prepared. Being able to answer the follow-up questions will show that you are an effective

title: How I Landed a Data Analyst Job in 4 Months
content: communicator, an important skill for a data analyst, and capable of taking on an analytics project from start to finish. Understanding the fine details of your work also allows you to provide more detailed answers. For example, an interviewer might ask if you have knowledge of any data visualization tools. Rather than just saying yes, it’s much more impactful if you can talk about that time you leveraged Tableau to build a dashboard. Behavioral Questions Image by NeONBRAND on Unplash Lastly,

title: How I Landed a Data Analyst Job in 4 Months
content: don’t forget to prepare for behavioral questions. In my experience, I was asked behavioral questions by every company I interviewed with and usually in multiple rounds. To prepare, I did research on common behavioral questions asked during interviews and practiced my answers out loud. Obviously, you don’t want to memorize a script, but, by practicing, you’re less likely to stumble during an interview. Try to think of responses that are relevant to data analytics and provide examples to back them

title: How I Landed a Data Analyst Job in 4 Months
content: up (see STAR Method). Conclusion Image by Filip Mroz on Unsplash By preparing in the above areas, you should be able to land a data analyst job in a few months. I cannot stress the importance of preparation – especially, for those who lack work experience. The reality is that if you lack experience, you will have to submit many applications before getting a hit – such was my experience. In light of this, you have to make the most of every interview you get. Happy interviewing and good luck!
