title: From economist to data analyst
content: Samuel Wondim stumbled his way into Data Analytics. But once he discovered it, he doubled down and taught himself the necessary skills. He was gracious enough to answer some questions about his career journey and learning strategies. What was your background before getting into data analytics? I graduated from Pepperdine in 2015 with a degree in Economics without having any idea what the next 5 years would look like. After graduating, I worked temp job after temp job in the hopes of stumbling

title: From economist to data analyst
content: into a career I was good at and enjoyed. Throughout that process I gained skills/experience that were integral in my current role—Excel and interpersonal communication. In 2017, I leveraged those skills and got my breakthrough moment when I was hired as a "Data Analyst" for a marketing company where I worked directly with one client: Epson. I put Data Analyst in quotations because, despite the title, I felt my role was more on the Business Intelligence side. What made want to pursue a career in

title: From economist to data analyst
content: data? I’m not sure how great my strategy was after college, but it did introduce me to data. Even after the first 6 or so months of being a "Data Analyst", the thought of having a career in data didn’t cross my mind. I honestly can’t remember the event that sparked my shift in focus for my future. But once I knew I wanted to figure out what my next 5–10 years would look like, I did a lot of research on the best careers of the future. As I’m sure you know, Data Science and Data Analytics were on

title: From economist to data analyst
content: the top of that list. There were a lot of reasons that I wanted to move on from my role at Epson. But one of the biggest drivers for me was always striving for self-improvement. Personally, there isn’t anything more gratifying in life than seeing the reward of hours of hard work. How did you approach self-learning? I took somecourses on Udemy for niche topics like Data Visualization, Time Series Analysis, SQL, etc.. But most of my learning was done for free by watching a LOT of YouTube! There is

title: From economist to data analyst
content: so much free content there. You just have to know what you’re looking for. Here are some channels I got value from: For all things Python: Tech with Tim Corey Schafer For statistics: ZedStatistics StatQuest with Josh Starmer For all things Data Science/ Data Analysis: Ken Jee Tina Huang To get practical experience, on top of completing a few Kaggle competitions here and there, I built an end-to-end data science project. I created a model that predicts the prices of houses in Los Angeles. I used

title: From economist to data analyst
content: the model to create a website that allows aspiring home buyers to estimate the price of the dream house based on features that are important to them (e.g. location, bedrooms, square footage, etc). I did all this with the guidance and support of my mentor Neal – who I found on SharpestMinds. Were you still working full-time while doing all of this? Yes, I was still working while self learning. If you’re lucky enough to have a position that is data science adjacent then you have the opportunity to

title: From economist to data analyst
content: take what you’re learning and apply it to your real job to get actual experience that you’re looking for. Don’t take it for granted, however. You should not be discouraged if you’re coming from another field. There are plenty of forums/communities you can join with like-minded individuals that can guide/motivate you on your self-learning journey. How did you find job openings to apply for? I tried to use every source that was made available to me. Here’s a breakdown of where I sourced the jobs

title: From economist to data analyst
content: I’ve applied for: LinkedIn: 45%* AngelList: 35% Indeed: 13% College Job Board: 5% SharpestMinds Job Board: 2% *LinkedIn includes both job posts & jobs referred to by recruiters. I received many more callbacks/interviews from AngelList and my college job board. Most of my job applications were from LinkedIn is because I found way more opportunities that interested me there. My current role at Disney was a result of recruiter reaching out to me on LinkedIn. I firmly believe years of preparation

title: From economist to data analyst
content: and failing at other interviews got me to that moment. What surprised you the most during interviews? The most surprising lesson I learned was how informal/relaxed most interviews are. If you’re like me (and many others in our field), you probably suffer from imposter-syndrome. The lack of confidence in your ability to perform for the job you’re applying for is a very common feeling. This feeling can cause a lot of anxiety leading up to your interviews; as it did for me. However, that anxious

title: From economist to data analyst
content: feeling quickly goes away minutes into the interview. With each succeeding interview I experienced, the minutes quickly became seconds; and the seconds ceased to exist. Eventually I didn’t feel any anxiety prior to the interview. What would you do differently, if you were to do it again? I wouldn’t change a thing. I’d continue to follow the "Do’s-and-Don’t’s" advice SharpestMinds gave me, as they are continually monitoring the data job market. I’d continue to soak in all the knowledge and

title: From economist to data analyst
content: experience my SharpestMinds mentor (shout-out to Neal!) bestowed upon me. I would, however, appreciate the journey a lot more. Protect your mental health and routinely take breaks. Trust the process; you’ll cross the finish line if you’re not cheating yourself. Samuel is a Senior Analyst, Marketing at Disney Streaming. You can connect with him on LinkedIn here.

title: 10 Most Important SQL Commands Every Data Analyst Needs to Know
content: Photo by Shunya Koide on Unsplash As a data analyst or data scientist, it doesn’t matter how good you are at creating fancy visualizations or how skilled you are at building complicated models – at its core, you need data in order to do those things. When working at a large company, these data are typically stored in a database such that everyone can easily access and query the data that they need to do their job. How do you query said data? Well, that’s where SQL comes in. SQL is short for

title: 10 Most Important SQL Commands Every Data Analyst Needs to Know
content: Structured Query Language and as the name suggests, it is a standardized language that is used to query or retrieve data from a relational database. Furthermore, it can also be used to perform various operations on the data such as filtering rows and columns as well as simple data manipulation. One of the earliest observations that I made when I started working as a data analyst was that everybody around me knew how to use SQL, and I mean literally everybody. Whether if you are an intern who

title: 10 Most Important SQL Commands Every Data Analyst Needs to Know
content: just recently joined the team or a senior analyst who has been around for a long time, this is a skill that everyone needs to know. This goes to show just how significant SQL is in the world of Data Science analytics. In light of this, I wanted to highlight the top 10 SQL commands in this blog post to help you get started on your journey with using SQL but more importantly, I will be demonstrating each command using practical examples in order to simulate the feeling of actually working with a

title: 10 Most Important SQL Commands Every Data Analyst Needs to Know
content: database. To do this, we will be using SQL Fiddle, a handy application for testing and sharing SQL queries online. For the purpose of this tutorial, I have created two mock tables called transaction and customers, which represent the transactions of a supermarket chain and customer profile respectively. 1. SELECT and FROM SELECT and FROM form the foundation of all SQL queries. The most basic SQL query will involve these two commands and as the query gets more complex, more commands will be added

title: 10 Most Important SQL Commands Every Data Analyst Needs to Know
content: on top of them. SELECT informs which columns you want to select whereas FROM specifies which table you want to query the data from. Let’s now look at some examples in relation to the transaction table. To view all the columns in the transaction table: SELECT * FROM transaction; Suppose we only want specific columns in the transaction table: SELECT transaction_id, purchase_date, sales FROM transaction; 2. DISTINCT DISTINCT is used to view the unique values in a column. For example, suppose we

title: 10 Most Important SQL Commands Every Data Analyst Needs to Know
content: would like to see the unique dates with transactions: SELECT DISTINCT purchase_date FROM transaction; 3. WHERE WHERE is used to filter rows that match a certain condition. Moreover, it is also often used with other operators such as AND, OR, BETWEEN, IN and LIKE to combine multiple conditions together. Here are some examples: SELECT * FROM transaction WHERE purchase_date = '2021-10-15'; SELECT * FROM transaction WHERE purchase_date = '2021-10-15' AND store_location = 'Melbourne CBD'; SELECT *

title: 10 Most Important SQL Commands Every Data Analyst Needs to Know
content: FROM transaction WHERE purchase_date = '2021-10-15' OR store_location = 'Melbourne CBD'; SELECT * FROM transaction WHERE store_location IN ('Richmond', 'Brunswick', 'Kew'); 4. % Wildcard The % wildcard is used in a LIKE operator to match string patterns. Before we look at how this wildcard works, let’s first examine the customer profile table. This table tells us the life stage and the premium status of a particular customer. SELECT * FROM customers; Suppose now we want to filter out the rows in

title: 10 Most Important SQL Commands Every Data Analyst Needs to Know
content: the customers’ table where the customer life stage starts with the word Young. SELECT * FROM customers  WHERE customer_lifestage LIKE 'Young%'; Similarly, if we want to view the rows where the customer life stage ends with the word families. SELECT * FROM customers  WHERE customer_lifestage LIKE '%families'; As you can see, SQL offers a quick and straightforward way to matching string patterns, which can be convenient in many situations when filtering out rows. 5. ORDER BY ORDER BY can be used

title: 10 Most Important SQL Commands Every Data Analyst Needs to Know
content: to sort the result of a query by a particular column either alphabetically or numerically. It can be ordered in two ways: DESC which is in descending order, or ASC which is in ascending order. Though you will notice that most people don’t write ASC in their queries as SQL sets this by default. To demonstrate this, suppose we would like to order the transactions in ascending order based on sales amount. SELECT store_location, sales FROM transaction  ORDER BY sales; Alternatively, we can also sort

title: 10 Most Important SQL Commands Every Data Analyst Needs to Know
content: the transactions in descending order based on sales amount. SELECT store_location, sales FROM transaction  ORDER BY sales DESC; 6. AS AS enables us to rename a column or table. Note that this will not directly alter the names in their original columns or tables. The given query will return the date column from the transaction table where _purchasedate is renamed to date. SELECT purchase_date as date FROM transaction; 7. CASE WHEN, ELSE and THEN If you have used any other programming languages

title: 10 Most Important SQL Commands Every Data Analyst Needs to Know
content: before, this is very similar to an if-else statement. Effectively, in plain English, the command sounds a little something like this: if a condition is satisfied, do this, otherwise do that. Let’s look at an example to solidify this idea. Suppose we want to create a new column that tells us if the sales amount of a particular transaction exceeds $20. SELECT transaction_id, sales, CASE WHEN sales < 20 THEN 'Sales amount is less than $20' ELSE 'Sales amount is greater than $20' END AS

title: 10 Most Important SQL Commands Every Data Analyst Needs to Know
content: sales_threshold  FROM transaction; 8. GROUP BY and aggregate functions GROUP BY will group data by their identical values. It is frequently used along with aggregate functions to summarise the attribute of a particular group of data. Aggregate functions, on the other hand, perform calculations on a range of values and return a single value. Some examples of aggregate functions include: COUNT: returns the total number of rows SUM: returns the sum of all the values MAX: returns the maximum value

title: 10 Most Important SQL Commands Every Data Analyst Needs to Know
content: MIN: returns the minimum value AVG: returns the average value Let’s now turn to some examples. Suppose we want to know the number of rows in the transaction dataset. SELECT COUNT(*) FROM transaction; What about the highest sales amount in the transaction dataset. SELECT MAX(sales) as max_sales FROM transaction; Lastly, what if we are interested to know the total sales of each day, rounded to the nearest dollar? SELECT purchase_date, ROUND(SUM(sales)) as total_sales  FROM transaction  GROUP BY

title: 10 Most Important SQL Commands Every Data Analyst Needs to Know
content: purchase_date; 9. JOIN Before we discuss the concept of joins, I think it is important that we first distinguish the difference between a primary key and a foreign key. In relational databases, a primary key is used to uniquely identify each row in a table. For instance, the primary key for the transaction table is the _transactionid column, whereas the primary key for the customer profile table is the _customerid column. A foreign key, on the other hand, provides a link between data in two

title: 10 Most Important SQL Commands Every Data Analyst Needs to Know
content: tables. Specifically, a foreign key in one table will link to the primary key in another table. For example, the _customerid column is a foreign key in the transaction table but it is a primary key in the customer profile table. Given the relationship between a primary key and a foreign key, we can perform a LEFT JOINin this particular scenario. There are other types of joins in Sql, such as INNER JOIN, RIGHT JOIN and FULL JOIN, which I won’t get to here. If you are interested to learn more,

title: 10 Most Important SQL Commands Every Data Analyst Needs to Know
content: check out this blog post for more details. For now, suppose we want to perform a LEFT JOIN on the transaction table based on the _customerid column. SELECT a.*, b.customer_lifestage, b.customer_premium FROM transaction AS a LEFT JOIN customers AS b ON a.customer_id = b.customer_id; It’s also good practice to always check the number of rows after we perform LEFT JOIN to make sure the new table has the same number of rows as the left table before the join, which in this case is the transaction

title: 10 Most Important SQL Commands Every Data Analyst Needs to Know
content: table. 10. UNION Last but certainly not least, UNION is used to combine query results from multiple SELECT statements. Note that the tables that you wish to union must have the same number of columns and equally important, the columns must be of the same data type. I have to admit, both the tables I have put together for this exercise might not be the best at illustrating the power of UNION, however, for the purpose of completeness, I will demonstrate it here. Suppose we want to union the

title: 10 Most Important SQL Commands Every Data Analyst Needs to Know
content: _customerid column with the _quantitypurchased column, both from the transaction table. SELECT customer_id AS sample_union FROM transaction  UNION SELECT quantity_purchased FROM transaction; With that, we conclude the 10 most important SQL commands that you need to get started with using SQL. I hope, through this blog post, you have gained a better understanding of what SQL is, and its significance in data science analytics but more importantly, realize that it is actually relatively easy to

title: 10 Most Important SQL Commands Every Data Analyst Needs to Know
content: learn once you get hold of the fundamentals. For any aspiring data analyst or data scientist, this is definitely one of the skills you should consider adding to your toolkit because SQL is here to stay. Don’t know what to read next? Here are some suggestions. Pandas Zero to Hero – A Beginner’s Tutorial to Using Pandas Five Basic Commands to Get Started with dplyr in R Beginner’s Introduction to NLP – Building a Spam Classifier

title: The data analyst skill you should be looking for
content: Are We All Missing One Crucial Data Analyst Interview Question? Antique Typewriter – Wikimedia Commons In my previous article titled "Is your data strategy missing the ‘Mark’?", I highlighted the responsibility of modern data leaders in building engagement between your business users and their data. It isn’t enough to provide the data and the tools to visualize or explore it. Users need first to have the literacy, then to be interested, and most often, the fastest path to creating that interest

title: The data analyst skill you should be looking for
content: is to construct a narrative. Narratives over numbers. If narratives are the key to communicating data, why aren’t you looking for analysts to write those narratives? As an analyst, if you can’t write, you can’t share. If you can’t share, your analysis has no value. Thousands of years ago, when humans first began to write stories down, they captured the oral stories passed through the generations. Over time, the drafting process was developed and cultivated. Authors crafted new stories as they

title: The data analyst skill you should be looking for
content: wrote them, perpetually read them back to themselves, and clarified the narrative for the most significant effect. Drafting was the key to refinement and honing a story that could be understood and related to by the audience. But, unfortunately, at that time, to be an author meant not only to be educated enough to read and write but also to be wealthy enough to buy paper, ink, and quills. Through time and an ever-increasing literacy rate, essential inventions helped propagate the ability and

title: The data analyst skill you should be looking for
content: ambition to tell stories. For example, the printing press meant stories could be shared faster and with more people. Typewriters improved speed by an exponential factor. As a result, authors could write more works more often and immediately share them. Computers brought the ability to craft a "soft" copy. A draft could be refined endlessly before ever needing a single drop of ink. Finally, the internet eliminated the need to print at all with digital publications. Gutenberg press – Wikimedia

title: The data analyst skill you should be looking for
content: Commons Now, drafting this, artificial intelligence runs with every letter I type, giving me spelling corrections, sentence structure adjustments to match a target delivery tone, and an analysis of the entire work for adherence to a pre-defined style guide. In our current world, we’re all continuously drafting. We’re writing our life stories (or what we wish they were) through social mediums. We write emails, slacks, and texts all day, every day. Even still, most of us are not great writers.

title: The data analyst skill you should be looking for
content: There isn’t a cohesive structure, no storyline to follow. Irrelevant details are injected while important notes are omitted. Most of us are awful writers. Writing is a critical skill, and even more so in a role wherein the expectation is to craft a narrative then clearly and consistently convey that narrative to a broad audience, all with varying degrees of information literacy. So why then are we not asking our data analyst candidates if they can write? Because most CS or CE programs only

title: The data analyst skill you should be looking for
content: require a general education level of language, literature, or writing-related credits, our data analysts are often no better or worse at crafting a narrative than anyone else. In considering the critical skillsets of a great analyst, we might all emphasize the visualization skills, the technical skills to query and explore the data, or the business acumen to understand and correlate the data to the business. But, maybe the skill we should be considering is "can they tell a story?". If you’re an

title: The data analyst skill you should be looking for
content: analyst yourself, think about the last dashboard you built or the slide deck you presented. Was the narrative present? Did you create a setting (i.e., the context of what was analyzed, why, etc.)? Was each step in the journey logical or foreshadowed? Finally, was the ending clear, and is there going to be a sequel? Whether you’re a team member or a leader (you don’t have to be a manager to be a leader), take the initiative and try having the group write a story to explain the antagonist (the

title: The data analyst skill you should be looking for
content: business challenge or question), the protagonist (the analyst(s)), the journey, and the ending of your initiative. As with any other writing, following a robust writing process will yield the best results. First, start on a whiteboard by listing all of the moving parts. Why did you, or are you going to, do this analysis? What were the key findings, data sets, and business users impacted? What logical conclusions might one anticipate? Many writers would typically move on to a bulleted outline at

title: The data analyst skill you should be looking for
content: this point, but if you’re an analyst, you may be a very visually oriented person. Storyboards, initially created by an animator named Webb Smith at Walt Disney, are great to piece together an outline. These can be as simple as post-its or blocks with each step of the analysis written on them. For example, "We found sales were up in this month." would then flow into "We classified the delta sales by product category for the month." The key is to sequence the events in an order that is both

title: The data analyst skill you should be looking for
content: logical and easy to follow. When you’re happy with your storyboard, write the first draft. Then? Revise. Revise. Revise. When everyone on the team is no less than thrilled with your draft, identify a test audience. Ideally, this is someone somewhat familiar with the domain but is not entirely aware of the analysis initiative (the goal is to have written something that can be consumed with no previous context). Get their feedback, then? Revise. Revise. Revise. You can repeat this process as many

title: The data analyst skill you should be looking for
content: times as is practical, but you’re likely to get some exceptional feedback from the first pass. The exercise of writing the story of your analysis may even make you rethink the approach you’ve taken or the conclusions you’ve drawn. The process can be a powerful tool and is valuable in planning initiatives yet to be executed, with the hypotheses acting as starting points to the storyboard or plot. Build. The. Narrative. Of course, the actual data needs to be layered in, and the intent here isn’t

title: The data analyst skill you should be looking for
content: to hand over pages upon pages as an analysis result. It’s up to you to distill everything down based on the goal, audience, etc., but if you’ve gone through the writing process and are crystal clear in your narrative, your findings will reach more ears. Engaged ears. Is your analysis a book you’d skim if you were a business user? Or one you wouldn’t be able to put down? Please consider supporting my writing by following me or signing up for Medium via my referral link. Thanks!

title: V2: What Makes a Great Data Analyst?
content: Photo by Katrina Wright via Unsplash In a recent article, I talked about what makes a great data analyst while focusing more on traits or characteristics and sprinkling in some hard skills/technologies. In this article, I will focus more on routine habits that can help you and discuss the impact they can have on your growth towards being a ‘top flight data analyst of the world, Craig!’ As a reminder, these bits of information have worked for myself based on my goals. You must first solve for

title: V2: What Makes a Great Data Analyst?
content: what role/routine duties you are seeking. With a goal in mind, finding the path that works best is much easier. Practice Asking Questions You might ask yourself, ‘Why do I need to practice asking questions?’. The crazy part about this is that you just asked a question! That was quick. Obviously, you’re a seasoned veteran at this. ‘The pods that were supposed to hear this did. It’ll kick in when it needs to.’ – The Great Philosopher, Randolph Dupree Doug Rose has one of, if not, my favorite

title: V2: What Makes a Great Data Analyst?
content: courses on LinkedIn titled ‘Learning Data Science: Ask Great Questions’. I highly recommend it for anyone working with data, whether it’s someone coding or someone using a report that is generated or a stakeholder that looks at visualizations regularly. Some of my favorite questions: What will break this? It’s not just coding bugs you have to worry about. Logic bugs exist too. What will this break? As noted in a previous article, don’t be the person recommending to cut ties with a new

title: V2: What Makes a Great Data Analyst?
content: distributor that’s skyrocketing sales just to save a few pennies on a particular KPI. What else can influence this? If time allows, go for the fruit higher up the tree. We can all ask questions, but do those questions close off OR encourage great ideas/follow-up questions? Strive for the latter. Do The Same Thing, But In a Different Way When learning to code, it’s easy to watch all sorts of videos or read tons of books, and that’s a great start. You can easily find online tutorials where you can

title: V2: What Makes a Great Data Analyst?
content: even type in some code to check results against questions asked. Find programs that aren’t looking for a fill-in-the-blank approach. You’re expected to be a MacGyver of sorts. A learning environment where you ‘parrot’ responses can take you only so far. Strive to be more like Emmet from ‘The Lego Movie’ and become a Master Builder. When you are more able to work in a way that you don’t need step-by-step instructions/built-in functions, you can then be more able to solve for more complex

title: V2: What Makes a Great Data Analyst?
content: situations. I’m not saying don’t use built-in functions. I’m just letting you know that MacGyver can do more with a shoestring, bubble gum, and dried out grass clippings than someone that only knows how to follow exact directions can with a Swiss Army knife. Some fun practice can be to replicate built-in Python functions. It’s crazy to think, but there are multiple routes you can take to sum up 3 numbers in a list. Finding the first X amount of prime numbers is a fun one as well. Work on solving

title: V2: What Makes a Great Data Analyst?
content: these problems and then come back to them after more experience and solve them using a different path. Take note of the section further down about adding some notes to your work though. It’ll save you some time when you revisit these problems. Talk About What You Do It’s very easy and common to sort of live in your own mind. You know what you’re talking about. Among all the factors of creating great dashboards, I think the most important one is frequent communication with your audience, who can be your teammate, manager, or executive. (Although, we also used a more popular tool like Mixpanel, which is way more efficient to

If the final dashboard is not what your end-user wants, you might waste your time arranging unwanted layouts or writing many unnecessary scripts if you’re using Metabase. Therefore, the most critical principle in creating dashboards is drafting and frequently communicating with your audience before building it. This is

Make experiments as simple as possible. In March and April, our marketing department made a campaign that brought in many first-time VIP users of a sudden. User operations

Therefore, I had designed an experiment in which the first-time VIP will have an exclusive discount as long as they finish ordering two VIP special product items. The rationale behind it was that if they could experience the benefits as VIP users as quickly as possible, then they might be more likely to want to remain the VIP status. As we are a startup, and our VIP status is

However, this became the reason that made this experiment not as successful as we expected. Since we started this test in mid-April, some first-time VIPs already finished purchasing one VIP unique item, and some didn’t buy anything. So, since there were these two groups of first-time VIPs, we needed to set up two in-app and push notification tracks in CleverTap, a

Each track will have 5 to 6 steps, in which the first step was the first time users open the app, then pop up the notification, then wait until the users purchase a VIP item, then send a push notification, and then repeat the process, until they finish purchasing two items. So, because of this, if a hypothesis can be supported by data evidence, the better. 3 Lessons on

content: Communication/Presentation 1. Explain the data sources first. When giving presentations to a data team, you should explain the data sources for a few reasons. The first one is that they all understand the data schema and can examine if your analysis matches perfectly with the data sources. The second reason is that they might recommend you to use other data sources that you didn’t consider but are helpful to your research. The third reason is that some senior colleagues in your team might know

If not, it would be hard to understand if this particular number is high or low – for example, retention of 30% after the first 30 days is high or low? When presenting a ratio, make sure to explain the meaning of the denominator since usually, the nuance is hiding in the context. Do you mean all the log-in users? Or paid users? title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: How to Start a Career as a Data Analyst from the Arts, and Why What you have that STEM graduates might not and what ‘big data’ has to gain from the arts Photo by Adam Wilson on Unsplash Isn’t it annoying when engineering students call themselves engineers? They’re getting ahead of themselves. It’s not like you hear medical students calling themselves doctors or arts students calling themselves baristas! So goes one of the jokes about arts degrees (source), the easy path through education for the

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: lazy or the thick that’s a lot of fun and leads nowhere. The place where it led for me, a graduate in French, was a career in analytics which I have found to be rewarding and well-suited to the abilities I gained during my time at university. It’s not an obvious connection to many but one I want to encourage more of in the world. I have been in the field for over a decade now and have experienced what it is to develop professional skills in the field from a starting point of no specific training

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: and what it is to practise analytics across agencies, start-ups and large corporates in London and Sydney. For the last three years, I have been in a position to recruit analysts for my corporate employers and have been able to challenge the norm for candidates to come with a degree in a STEM subject, with evidence from my own experience that analytics in business has ample use for aptitudes gained in the study of the humanities (I prefer the term ‘humanities’ to ‘arts’ but I am using them

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: interchangeably here). In this article, I will attempt to explain what these aptitudes are, how they fit into analytics and where to start for those considering a career in analytics from non-STEM backgrounds. I hope to inspire graduates with the right inclinations to give it a shot, convince hiring managers to think more openly about the profiles they consider, and play a part generally in bringing the humanities and the sciences closer together. What is a ‘data analyst’? Firstly, what do I

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: mean by a data analyst here? What does one do with their time? I would say it’s fair to characterise the world of analytics as consisting of three core disciplines right now, typically split into the labels of ‘Data Analyst’, ‘Data Engineer’ and ‘Data Scientist’. In the simplest terms, the Data Analyst explores data for insights that can be used for business decision making, the Data Engineer manages the computing tools necessary for the collection, storage and access of ‘big’ data, and the Data

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: Scientist builds software that can be used by the business to make predictions, personalise recommendations and more. I won’t describe the other two disciplines in any more detail here, suffice to say that they are specialised and deeply technical roles that would probably not suit a generalist graduate (though the lines are often blurred at an entry level). But for more on the distinctions between the three disciplines, here is a good article that compares job ads for each role. The Data

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: Analyst role on the other hand is more accessible because novices with a comparatively simple knowledge of techniques can bring value to an organisation through other aptitudes such as good communication or an eye for insight. We can liken the role to a journalist uncovering a story, building a body of evidence to prove a hypothesis and captivating their readers through the use of persuasive storytelling. For the Data Analyst, the evidence would generally be based on numerical data and the

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: storytelling led by data visualisation but the underlying quest and patterns of thinking are similar. (For a classic example of engaging data storytelling, see Hans Rosling’s TED talk). Photo by Caspar Camille Rubin on Unsplash Stories concealed in the data might be a spike in demand for a product that can be tied to certain circumstances (like food deliveries on rainy days) or the particular appeal of a product to certain types of audiences (like coffee for the cycling community). A business

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: decision the analyst could help to make in these instances might be to increase resources for next time we anticipate such an event or to target advertising to those communities. The tools used for Data Analysis typically involve spreadsheets (e.g. Excel, Google Sheets), a data visualisation tool (e.g. Tableau, Google Data Studio) and SQL code. You can find more on how to get started with these tools later on in the article. Python and R are also referenced a lot in connection to the role and

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: are particularly useful for statistical analysis and importing publicly available data from the internet, though I would say they are inessential to begin with and a nice-to-have even at senior levels despite their prevalence in job ads. In a typical week, an experienced data analyst might: Meet with decision makers in their organisation to discuss questions they have (e.g. what made my last marketing campaign so successful? What are the reasons people don’t repeat purchases with us?) and

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: consult on approaches to answering them using available data. Explore and clean datasets using any of the tools outlined above. ‘Cleaning’ is the process of getting messy data to line up and this is typically what takes the most time in analysing a dataset. (To give a simple example, a column of data showing customers’ gender might mix ‘F’ and ‘female’ and ‘Female’ which all indicate the same thing but are different as far as the data is concerned. To clean this, we might convert all of these to

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: ‘F’.) Spend time doing research to understand how the data they are working with is collected. For example, in a dataset of marketing results with revenue broken down by the channels that drove the purchases, how exactly are we attributing the purchase to a social media ad, an email newsletter etc? What if the customer saw multiple ads from multiple channels before they chose to make the purchase? Design experiments to test hypotheses. Present findings to decision makers with the use of visual

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: storytelling and make suggestions on actions to take based on the insight. As an analyst deepens their technical capabilities and accumulates domain knowledge, the potential complexity of their analysis will increase, but none of this will be effective if their audience fails to understand them or glimpse the ‘so what?’ behind all the analysis. And this is where the ability to see the wood for the trees and communicate persuasively becomes paramount. It is a hurdle that trips up many of the

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: technically brilliant types and a key area in which a humanities graduate might find they have an advantage. What else can they bring? What do the humanities bring to data analytics? In 2020, following the Australian government’s defunding of the humanities in tertiary Education, the Guardian Australia made a shout out for comments to humanities graduates asking how their degree equipped them for work. What do you think the core themes were in the comments? Can you guess which two-word term

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: encapsulating the values of the humanities came up more than any other across all the comments (90 times across 484 comments to be exact)? Photo by Giammarco on Unsplash Before we get to the answer, here is a comment that exemplifies the main themes that came through from readers: The degree gave me the tools to think for myself, question everything that I was being told and come to my own conclusions about what was really going on[…] Communication skills, being able to write clearly,

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: articulately and persuasively, are consistently ranked as one of the most important attributes by employers looking for new employees. Strangely, however, they don’t seem to make the connection between the skills they’re looking for and arts graduates. [Bizkit] And here is one from a commenter working in a numerate field we tend to associate with STEM backgrounds: I majored in English and Classical literature. I spent most of my career in funds management. I ran two for major listed and private

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: companies and spent over a decade with one of Australia’s leading fund managers. My lack of accounting training was more than compensated for by my critical assessment skills. Arts degrees teach you how to learn and think critically – more people should try it. __ [mganci23] And there it is: ‘think critically’. In a world where we are faced with a deluge of information and uncertain facts, how do we know what to trust and how to make decisions? The term and its variations came up 90 times across

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: 484 top-level comments, with much of the discussion in the other comments also drawing on the same idea. It’s the top bigram (two-word combination) by a long shot, excluding the terms ‘arts degree’ and ‘humanities degree’, and in a count of all single word frequencies (which was less useful here for picking out key themes), variations on ‘thinking’ ranked notably high. Here is the dataset if you would like to take a look. Image by author So why is ‘critical thinking’ a hallmark of the

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: humanities, and is it really not acquired as part of a STEM education? I imagine there will be STEM graduates ready to staunchly defend their critical thinking abilities gained from their time studying or otherwise, but I think there is enough evidence to draw on that suggests there is some shortage of it in the way STEM is broadly taught. There is a much discussed replication crisis unfolding in the social sciences at the moment which casts doubt on the fundamental approach that scientists are

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: taking in drawing conclusions, and it seems like parts of the scientific community have become habituated to using statistical tools they don’t fully understand. David Epstein, a critic of poor scientific research, suggests that shallow thinking is endemic in science from the way it is learned in universities, claiming in his book Range: Like many a grad student, I had a big database and hit a computer button to run a common statistical analysis, never having been taught to think deeply (or at

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: all) about how that statistical analysis even worked. The stat program spit out a number summarily deemed ‘statistically significant.’ Unfortunately, it was almost certainly a false positive because I did not understand the limitations of the statistical test in the context in which I applied it. Nor did the scientists who reviewed the work[…] I rushed into extremely specialized scientific research without having learned scientific reasoning. (And then I was rewarded for it, with a master’s

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: degree). And it is easy to imagine in degrees like engineering and computer science that students are directed towards rules-based thinking, building up knowledge of how things fit together and dexterity in solving logical problems – valuable skills, no doubt. But how far will these skills help them in the world of human decision making where there often aren’t straight answers to problems, or there are missing facts, or there are severe limits to time in which to come to conclusions? How to

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: weigh up evidence amidst uncertainty, form a position and explain it is the domain of the humanities and as the tide of STEM has been rising, so too is emerging a counter pressure from the humanities urging for balance. A good focal point for this can be found in the STEAM movement which advocates for the adding of ‘A’ for ‘Arts’ to STEM education to cultivate more human-centric thinking. But how does this relate to data analytics? Isn’t the use of data basically a maths problem? No, and this is

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: where there is still a massive misperception in what analytics entails in practice. The biggest misperception, which the industry benefits from upholding, is that what the data tells us are objective facts. In reality, there is uncertainty and subjectivity in the use of data (see Jonathan Choi’s discussion for a good starting point on this), with plenty of room for bending data to artificially support an agenda as highlighted in books such as A Field Guide to Lies (also published under the title

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: Weaponized Lies) and Calling Bullshit. Experienced analysts in big organisations will likely be all too familiar with the request to back up a statement with supporting data, with the opportunity perhaps to challenge it but not enough time available to do so. Often when talking about the role the humanities might play in data analysis, we jump to the communication aspects, but another key aptitude is a mindset of questioning how the data will be used (leading to the ‘so what?’) and, just as

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: importantly, where the data has come from. There is a dictum in computer science Garbage In Garbage Out, but rare is the analyst who questions how valid the data is in the first place or makes the data’s origin a subject of their inquiry. There are often biases or problems in the way data is collected in the first place that might change our interpretation of the data and, obvious though this might sound, analysts all too often fail to critically examine their source of information. Critical

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: thinking is a habit of mind that is difficult to teach. The techniques for manipulating data, whether through code or other tools, are easier. Why job ads for data analyst positions ask for a STEM degree Photo by ThisisEngineering RAEng on Unsplash Every job in analytics I have been offered since my first has stipulated the requirement for a degree in maths, computer science, statistics, economics and the like, which I don’t have. But this has never got in the way. In Australia, where the ethos

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: of going to university seems to be more about vocational training than it is in the UK, colleagues have been surprised about my degree background. When I make new connections on LinkedIn, I am curious to check their educational backgrounds, and I can’t think of a single analyst I’ve met in Australia who doesn’t have a STEM or business-related degree. In the UK, where employers are less prescriptive over undergraduate fields of study, there is more of a mix of backgrounds. (Curiously, software

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: developers seem to come from far more eccentric backgrounds). I don’t doubt that STEM degrees provide some practical tools for the job and a leg up for securing the first role, but I want others to know that most of these degrees don’t directly equip graduates for the job. Mathematicians are not taught how to evaluate the performance of marketing campaigns. Computer scientists are not taught how to conduct A/B tests in a business. They pick these things up on the job and employers look for

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: graduates who are quick to learn, pleasant to teach and who will get on well with everyone as they grow into the role. The technical skills essential for data analysis can be learned on the job to a sufficiently useful standard fairly quickly and career progression very soon starts to focus on building domain knowledge (i.e. how your industry works, what the latest trends are) and improving ‘soft skills’, which university degrees do not cover in any relevant depth. That’s not to say that STEM is

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: irrelevant to this role – the scientific method and certain specifics such as an understanding of statistics are very much useful – but my point is that it doesn’t directly prepare you for this job and there are qualities from the humanities that are also useful and undervalued. Ultimately, it is a role that suits people who have range. And it might help job seekers to understand that the primary reason STEM is demanded in job ads is they act as a filter that helps reduce the number of

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: applications that recruiters have to review. For the reason that anyone is free to apply for a publicly advertised job, big companies might receive hundreds of applications and it would simply be impossible to review every one, so they need a way to maximise their chance of finding good candidates within their time limits. Adding the requirement of a STEM degree up front for this purpose makes the assumption that there is a higher likelihood of a STEM applicant being a good fit for the role than

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: a humanities applicant. The assumed composition of the applicant pool might look something like the below. (The distributions are hypothetical and the aim of this is to help conceptualise the decision making heuristics that hiring managers use. It is not intended as insight into the sizes and shapes of the talent pool.) Image by author The bars represent distributions of humanities and STEM graduates in terms of their likelihood of success in the role of a junior data analyst. We are assuming

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: the average STEM grad has a higher likelihood of success in the role than the average humanities grad, but the suitability of graduates will be variable within each group and some humanities grads will be more suitable than many STEM grads. Despite some good humanities candidates at the upper end of the distribution, if employers are limited in the time they can take to consider applicants, picking only from the green pool would be a reasonable time-saving measure. Image by author But what about

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: the exceptional humanities graduates in the right tail of the yellow distribution? Unfortunately, missing out on them is the tradeoff of using the filter. They are rejected not because they are actually unsuitable for the role but because they are unsuitable for the employer’s consideration given their time constraints and the heuristics they’ve put in play. (As an interesting aside, it has been suggested a similar process is action with the bad English grammar of email scammers – those who

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: aren’t likely to fall for it will be suspicious of the poor writing and drop off instantly, thus minimising the time the scammers might waste in follow-up work with bait that ultimately doesn’t pay.) Image by author So, job seekers, understand that a failure to get past the screening stage of an application may not be about your potential in the role and career but about the practical limitations of employers considering every application. Sadly, the current heuristic for using STEM is an

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: effective one so those who fall victim to it need another route in. Getting a first job in analytics Regardless of your background, here are some tips for entering the field if the ‘front door’ is proving difficult. Start studying online My entry into analytics was aided by some self-teaching via books. The demand for data analysts in industry has since ballooned and so has the amount of excellent learning resources online. Diving into some learning will not only give you skills that will be

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: directly useful in a data analytics career but also test whether you will indeed enjoy the career or not. My go-to free online resource I point beginners to is Mode’s excellent primer on SQL. For more expansive, paid options I would suggest diving into Datacamp’s interactive SQL tutorials or Google’s data analytics course on Coursera which seems to be getting a lot of attention right now. Give yourself about 10 hours of study a week for 3 months and you will have got a good taste of what is

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: involved and some useful skills to exhibit in your job applications, as well as evidence of your motivation. Network Follow analytics agencies and individuals working in analytics on LinkedIn and Twitter. Don’t hesitate to ask strangers for advice and don’t be discouraged if you mostly don’t hear back. What they post will give you a good idea of the topics that are currently front of mind in the community and there will often be links to free webinars and local events you can join. Look up

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: analytics events in your local city on meetup.com (I recommend ‘Digital Analytics Wednesday’ or ‘Data & Analytics Wednesday’ which takes place in many major cities around the world once a month). Ask people you know to introduce you to analysts that they know and get their advice. Enter analytics via other roles You would be hard pressed to find a business function in which data isn’t useful. Don’t feel like you’re taking a wrong turn by applying for other roles and, once in, find ways to get

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: exposure to data. Volunteer to clean up a spreadsheet or challenge yourself to improve a part of your function with the use of data. Perhaps you could organise an internal survey and create a pack for your team visualising the results. Make contact with people in your organisation who are performing data analysis in their functions. Keep at the online courses in the evenings. Closing thoughts I intended this article primarily for job seekers coming from the arts and the fact that you found your

title: How to start a career as a data analyst from a background in the arts, and why
content: way to this article probably means that you have already considered this as a direction in your life. I hope I have been able to inspire you to take the plunge and convince you that this could be a viable option for you despite all the signs pointing otherwise. For others, particularly in business, I hope this has given you some food for thought on the challenges of data analysis in a dynamic, fast-moving environment and the need for more critical thinking.

title: Behind the Scenes of a Data Analyst Recruiting Process
content: Earlier this year I was involved with the recruiting process for a new data analyst position on my team. I’ve interviewed for data analyst jobs and been an interviewer at onsite interviews but this was the first time I was part of the hiring process from beginning to end. Today I want to give you a behind the scenes look at the recruiting process and how you can leverage this information from both sides – as the hiring manager or the job applicant. Job Description The job description was a wish

title: Behind the Scenes of a Data Analyst Recruiting Process
content: list of what we wanted in a candidate. We deferred to HR to help us screen for applicants meeting the job requirements. Our mistake was not relaying to HR the skills we felt were the most important. This resulted in unqualified candidates passing the initial HR interview and proceeding to an interview with my manager. Let’s take a look at the skills needed in this hybrid data analyst/data scientist role. A proven track record of initiating and delivering actionable analyses/recommendations in

title: Behind the Scenes of a Data Analyst Recruiting Process
content: order to drive business impact Some experience building data science models to provide deeper insights Excellent communication skills (technical and non-technical) and comfort working with high-level stakeholders Recruiting tip: HR and the hiring manager should align on the most important skills necessary for success in the role. Provide pre-qualifying questions for HR to assess if the candidate has the experience that aligns with those skills. Using the example above, HR can ask candidates to

title: Behind the Scenes of a Data Analyst Recruiting Process
content: describe a time when they provided recommendations that drove business impact, an example of insights gained from a Machine Learning model, and their approach explaining data results to different audiences to assess their communication skills. Adding the pre-qualifying questions helped us filter out candidates in the initial HR interview and saved my manager time from having to talk to candidates that didn’t have the necessary skills. Applicant tip: Focus on the top 2 to 3 required skills in job

title: Behind the Scenes of a Data Analyst Recruiting Process
content: descriptions. If there’s a section that says "nice to have" check if you have any of the ones listed. On your resume, emphasize experience matching the top skills in the job description to increase your chances of getting an interview. During your HR or hiring manager interview, discuss examples of when you demonstrated those top skills when asked to describe your job experience. This will help show how your experience aligns with the needs of the role. Applicants HR placed the job on commonly

title: Behind the Scenes of a Data Analyst Recruiting Process
content: used job sites such as Glassdoor and LinkedIn but we didn’t get many applicants. My theory was because we were recruiting for a senior-level role and there weren’t as many people with the 6+ years of experience we required. The role asked for mentoring junior analysts and had the potential to become a manager position. I suggested we change the job title from "senior analyst" to "senior manager" to attract senior analysts looking to become a manager. This increased the number of applicants but

title: Behind the Scenes of a Data Analyst Recruiting Process
content: the downside was we had managers applying for the role when we needed a hands-on senior analyst with the potential to become a manager. We did get a few great candidates, one of which we ended up hiring. Recruiting tip: If you’re not getting enough qualified applicants for the role, consider listing the job with a different title or modifying the requirements of the role to attract more people to apply. We initially asked for 10+ years of experience and lowered it to 6+ to increase our applicant

title: Behind the Scenes of a Data Analyst Recruiting Process
content: pool. Applicant tip: LinkedIn shows the number of applicants for jobs. Find ones with a low number of applicants and apply to those jobs to increase your chances of getting noticed. If you see a job is reposted for the same company most likely they’re not getting qualified applicants. Take advantage of this to highlight your experience that aligns with the required skills. Take Home Test We had a take home test that was given to every candidate that passed the HR and hiring manager interviews.

title: Behind the Scenes of a Data Analyst Recruiting Process
content: This helped us assess how the candidate would approach a real-life business problem. Some companies prefer technical interviews and ask candidates to answer questions on the spot. We didn’t feel it would be indicative of future performance because you can practice for these types of tests online and pass but given a real-life scenario they may fail. We were able to filter out many candidates with the take home test that we wouldn’t have been able to otherwise during the phone interviews.

title: Behind the Scenes of a Data Analyst Recruiting Process
content: Recruiting tip: Assess technical and business acumen with a take home test or technical interview. Make sure the test will help screen out candidates that won’t be successful in the role. Applicant tip: Normally HR will notify you of what you’ll be tested on. In the past, I was told in advance if it was a SQL, Python, or a combination test. Use online resources to practice your technical skills if needed. Final Thoughts From beginning to end our recruiting process took about 4 months. We ended

title: Behind the Scenes of a Data Analyst Recruiting Process
content: up hiring a wonderful analyst for our team and I couldn’t have been happier when HR told us the offer was accepted. The lessons learned along the way were definitely helpful to refine the process for future data analysts we planned to hire. I also gained new insights being part of the recruiting process that wouldn’t have occurred to me as a job applicant. I hope this behind the scenes look has helped you gain a new perspective in the recruiting process the next time you hire or apply for a data

title: 4 Non-tech Books I recommend to any Data Analyst
content: Photo by Clarisse Meyer on Unsplash During my first years of working in the area of Data Analytics, I read many books that I found very helpful in making me a better Data Analyst. Among them, 4 books stand out, which I would recommend to anyone who wants to enter this area or continue to develop. All the books that are named here are non-tech. None of them talk about programming skills (SQL, R, Python, etc) or statistics – there are already many reading lists that I would highly recommend as

title: 4 Non-tech Books I recommend to any Data Analyst
content: this one! In my post, I would like to focus on the books that helped me improve my problem-solving skills, structured thinking & communication, business sense, and stakeholder management, which are very valuable qualities of a great Data Analyst as I summarised in a previous post. These 4 books are: ❓ Start with Why, which trains you to start by asking good questions and become more decision-driven. 🪜 The Pyramid Principle, which teaches you how to define and solve problems in a structured

title: 4 Non-tech Books I recommend to any Data Analyst
content: manner and how to present your insights in an effective way. 📈 Lean Analytics, which presents the metric systems under six business models as well as the benchmarks, making it a perfect material for preparing analyst interviews. 🛒 Freakonomics, which helps those without a business/economics background to formulate better hypotheses and validate them. Below you could find my personal takeaways from these books. Let’s get started! Start with Why: How Great Leaders Inspire Everyone to Take Action

title: 4 Non-tech Books I recommend to any Data Analyst
content: Photo by Zach Lucero on Unsplash In this book Simon Sinek shared many examples of why some organizations succeed and why others don’t (my favorite one is Southwest Airlines) and eventually present the theory of the Golden Circle. The main idea is that, if you are able to effectively communicate why you do what you do, rather than what you are doing and how you do it, is a very impactful way to communicate with other humans and inspire them to follow you. From the very first pages, the book may

title: 4 Non-tech Books I recommend to any Data Analyst
content: seem counter-intuitive to any data person since, in the very first chapter, the author states that more data or information does not necessarily lead to better decisions, especially when people start with false assumptions. However, when I look back to my path as a Data Analyst, I realize that this message actually makes perfect sense. As I shared in my previous post, I believe that as a data person, I create value for my team not by executing exactly the wishes of my colleagues but by helping

title: 4 Non-tech Books I recommend to any Data Analyst
content: them achieve their ultimate goals. This means that sometimes I need to stop gathering data to answer those ill-formatted questions or hypotheses, and instead help people to ask good questions – questions that are truly relevant to the ultimate goals. In the end, "starting with goals" is an incredibly valuable skill that marks the transition from a Junior to a Senior Data Analyst. This learning echoes with a profound post I recently read, where the author points out the differences between

title: 4 Non-tech Books I recommend to any Data Analyst
content: decision-driven analytics and data-driven analytics and argues for being more decision-driven, that is, to start with questions/hypotheses, not data; to search first wide instead of deep; and to be more readily challenged than perpetuated. Overall, I believe that this book brings unique value to anyone who is or wants to be a Data Analyst, in a way that it helps you understand why good questions matter more than good answers and eventually prepares you to be more decision-driven than data-

title: 4 Non-tech Books I recommend to any Data Analyst
content: driven. The Pyramid Principle: Logic in Writing and Thinking Photo by Les Anderson on Unsplash Those who have read my previous posts can already tell how much I love this book! As a true advocate, I could not recommend this book more. In fact, I have even hosted a Browbag session with my team to share my learnings. If you are interested, have a look here! There are two major things from this book that I found particularly helpful in my career as a data person. First of all, there are many tips

title: 4 Non-tech Books I recommend to any Data Analyst
content: that help build structured thinking. The most well-known MECE principle, i.e., Mutually Exclusive, Collectively Exhaustive, is a very powerful framework for any Data Analyst to dissect the problem and formulate hypotheses for second-order questions like "Why is there a drop in sales revenue?" or "Why do we see an increase in churn rate?". In addition, the Sequential Analysis and the SCQ framework help one to quickly define and scope problems, which is the key to any successful problem-solving!

title: 4 Non-tech Books I recommend to any Data Analyst
content: Second, the book also shares many best practices for presenting and communicating insights, which is a daily job for every Data Analyst. For example, always put your conclusion first in any presentation to help your audiences to get the key idea, usually a "what", at the first sight, and let them decide on their own whether or when they want to know more details behind the "what". Another trick is to always limit your supporting arguments to a maximum of three (i.e. the Rule of Three), which

title: 4 Non-tech Books I recommend to any Data Analyst
content: helps your arguments get attention and become memorable. If you would like to know more about how I applied what I’ve learned from this book in my daily presentation of insights, feel free to check this post! Lean Analytics: Use Data to Build a Better Startup Faster (Lean Series) Photo by Nick Fewings on Unsplash This book is a classic in the world of startup and product analytics so I would not expand too much here. 🙂 Personally, what I found most valuable from the book are the criteria of good

title: 4 Non-tech Books I recommend to any Data Analyst
content: KPIs and the concept of The One Metric That Matters. I wrote a post on how we defined and measured the OMTM in our case – check out here! Another thing I want to highlight is that the book provides unique value to a Data Analyst, especially those who are in their early career stage. Imagine that you have just spent 1–2 years at a company and are looking for new opportunities, especially those from a different business model, the metric systems under six business models (i.e., e-commerce, SaaS,

title: 4 Non-tech Books I recommend to any Data Analyst
content: free app, media, UGC, marketplace) as well as the benchmarks for these metrics are best sources to prepare for interviews and challenge tests when he/she does not have practical work experience in a different area. Freakonomics: A Rogue Economist Explores the Hidden Side of Everything Photo by Brooke Cagle on Unsplash Technically speaking, I just started to read this book recently and haven’t finished it yet. I’ve heard a lot about this book before, but I did not really read it since I have

title: 4 Non-tech Books I recommend to any Data Analyst
content: received formal training in the area of economics and econometrics during my bachelor’s study. That said, I realized that it was actually a pity that I did not read this book before! It gives tons of real-life examples and explains the mechanism behind those phenomena in an easily digestible manner. It is a great introductory book for anyone who has not received training in economics. What unique value does it bring to one who has a passion for data analytics? Well, very often Data Analysts are

title: 4 Non-tech Books I recommend to any Data Analyst
content: able to find correlations or patterns in a huge amount of data using different techniques such as scatterplots, regression, statistical tests, etc. What is missing sometimes, as I personally observed from our hiring process, is the ability to propose the second-order hypotheses behind the observed patterns. For instance, when an analyst spots from a bar plot that users with higher income generate more revenue for our business, we also expect him/her to propose hypotheses that could explain this

title: 4 Non-tech Books I recommend to any Data Analyst
content: pattern, e.g., people with higher income have more valuable properties so they need more insurances. The ability to incessantly create good hypotheses and try to validate them is a highly valued trait of a good Data Analyst. This book provides many practical examples in this exact case! For instance, it shares a study that investigates the relationship between many factors and students’ academic performance. In addition to presenting the results from the regression model, the author also tries

title: 4 Non-tech Books I recommend to any Data Analyst
content: to analyze why some factors are relevant (i.e., the number of books in a family is positively correlated with kids’ performance) and some are not (i.e., reading books to the kids is not correlated) – the former one is indicative of parents’ education while the latter is simply a behavior that can be easily copied. Therefore, I would highly recommend this book to anyone who aspires to start a career as a Data Analyst without a business or economics background! What books would you recommend to a

title: 4 Non-tech Books I recommend to any Data Analyst
content: (to-be) Data Analyst?

title: How Selling Shoes Made Me a Better Data Analyst
content: As a sophomore in high school, I started working at a local running store. I was on the cross country and track teams, an obsessive nerd when it came to running gear, and so it only made sense to find a job that combined both. At the shop, I spent most of my time working one-on-one with customers to help fit them with shoes and occasionally select various apparel. When I say I was an obsessive nerd on running gear, I truly mean it. I could tell you the stack heights of every shoe, the chemical

title: How Selling Shoes Made Me a Better Data Analyst
content: compounds that made up the soles, and at one point had every color code memorized for 50+ models. I spent most days wearing 2–3 different pairs of shoes while I worked, "product testing" the models so I could speak to them later. Image by Author Working in a running store brought a wide variety of customers in. There were plenty of high school and college runners, older adults who had been running for a while, new-to-running persons trying on their first shoes, and plenty of other variations.

title: How Selling Shoes Made Me a Better Data Analyst
content: Given the variety of the customer base, I was involved in a lot of different interactions and as a result, really honed my ability to sell shoes. The mindset I held when selling shoes was that I never particularly cared if an individual bought shoes. Now, that may sound counterintuitive, but there’s a reason for it. My focus was on finding someone a product that would create a positive experience between them and running. Forcing someone to buy a shoe wasn’t in their best interest, and

title: How Selling Shoes Made Me a Better Data Analyst
content: consequently wasn’t in mine. So instead of being a "How can I sell this shoe?" question, it was "How can I find the right product for this individual?". This is where things get interesting. When working with a customer, it’s important to know your audience. If I was working with an experience, competitive runner, the conversation would be very different than if I was working with a first-time shoe buyer. In the first case, I might dive more into some of the technical specifications, explaining

title: How Selling Shoes Made Me a Better Data Analyst
content: the weight differences, material styles, and how they would impact running. In the latter situation, the conversation usually goes a bit differently. Instead of explaining the difference between engineered mesh, EVA foam, and the likes, I would frequently explain things at a higher level, comparing shoes to pillows and springs. The basic information being communicated was still the same, but the format was different. Knowing who you’re talking to is a huge aspect of sales and being able to put

title: How Selling Shoes Made Me a Better Data Analyst
content: technical language into a comfortable conversation makes it easier to solve the problem at hand. So how does any of this relate to data analytics? Well, the problems encountered in data analytics are pretty much the same as in a running shop. In data, you can get as technical (or as non-technical) as you want, building anything from a pie chart to a neural network. However, the solution(s) you end with depend on… Who is your audience? What do they really need? In many cases, the information

title: How Selling Shoes Made Me a Better Data Analyst
content: presented only matters if you get buy-in from the audience. If your boss comes from a non-technical background and you throw up slides of t-tests, ANOVA Analysis, and hyperparameter tuning, you’re going to lose them real quick. And if they don’t buy in, then the work you’re doing really doesn’t matter because it never makes it off your desk. So much like I sold shoes, I now have to sell Data analysis. While it’s important to be able to do good data analysis and have strong knowledge of the

title: How Selling Shoes Made Me a Better Data Analyst
content: technical skills required, it’s arguably equally (or more) important to be able to sell and communicate that analysis. At the end of the day, if those around you aren’t willing to buy into using data, all the analysis in the world is meaningless. When working with the data, think about how you would sell it to someone. What benefits does it drive? How does it fit their need(s)? How easy is it to understand? Working on a problem in data is much like selling shoes. You have to understand your

title: How Selling Shoes Made Me a Better Data Analyst
content: client’s background to determine how you’ll present information to them. You need to be able to translate that technical information into something understandable that makes sense. Sometimes that means statistical deep-dives with scatterplots, autocorrelation graphs, and a table of model parameters. Other times it means a bar graph. And while the prior may seem like it conveys more information, it only does so if your audience understands it and can connect it to the problem. A mountain of

title: How Selling Shoes Made Me a Better Data Analyst
content: information is no better than a single fact if the client can’t understand it. It’s easy to get caught up in the allure of data, thinking that the quality of the analyst is derived from the depth of their work. What many (young) analysts often don’t realize is that unlike school, where you’re often required to perform pages of analysis, the real world focuses on impact, and impact is tied to understanding. With that in mind, how are you going to "sell" your data?

title: How to Study for the IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate
content: An overview of how to succeed in the "original" data analyst professional certificate Photo by PolaroMagnet on Unsplash The big brother to the Google Data Analytics Professional Certificate, the IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate offers the Python-based counterpart to the same formula: an online, self-paced data analyst course provided by a historical name in the tech game. title: How to Study for the IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate
content: willingness to learn. If the past year and a bit have taught us anything, it’s that career happiness is more important than staying in a comfort zone. Despite uncertainty about the future, 1 in 4 workers is considering quitting their job after the pandemic, a definite sign that shows that people are putting themselves first. What better time than right now to begin upskilling in a way that can help guarantee you better employment options? With 72,633 open data analyst roles in the United States

title: How to Study for the IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate
content: with a median salary of $74,440 and a 9% projected 10-year growth rate, this reasonably priced, self-paced, and easily accessible course is the perfect way to get your foot in the door without having to make massive life changes. What is the IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate? The IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate is a completely online and self-paced professional training course designed by IBM that prepares you to become a junior data analyst. The program is composed of 9

title: How to Study for the IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate
content: courses that can be completed in 11 months with less than 3 hours put in every week. The program is 100% online, allowing you to learn at your own pace. The program is also offered in 11 languages (English, Arabic, French, Portuguese (European), Italian, Vietnamese, German, Russian, Spanish, Turkish, and Persian), making it accessible to people on all continents. The courses are completed through the online learning platform, Coursera. What do you learn? Over the course of the IBM Data Analyst

content: Professional Certificate, you will learn all of the skills required for you to enter an entry-level data analyst position.
