From there, you will begin to learn the tools of the trade

title: How to Study for the IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate
content: necessary for data cleaning, organizing, analyzing, and visualizing, including: Spreadsheets (for basic level data wrangling, cleaning, analyzing, filtering, and sorting) Excel and IBM Cognos Analytics (for data visualization and dashboards) Python (for data structures and analyses) SQL (for wrangling, organizing, and querying data) Pandas, Numpy, and Scipy (for manipulating, analyzing, and using machine learning algorithms) Matplotlib, Seaborn, and Folium (for data visualizations) By enrolling

title: How to Study for the IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate
content: in this program, you also gain access to Coursera Career Services, where you will be able to learn about the latest hiring trends, get personalized interview training, and talk with recruiting experts. Furthermore, IBM provides several project opportunities throughout the course (including a final capstone project) that can be used to bolster your professional portfolio. What is the course curriculum? IBM has created 9 courses that will guide you through becoming a proficient junior data

title: How to Study for the IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate
content: analyst. Course 1: Introduction to Data Analytics This course starts with a gentle introduction to the concepts of data analysis, the role of a Data Analyst, and the tools used to perform daily functions. At the end of this course, you will have an understanding of the data ecosystem, the basics of data analysis, and the soft skills required to be an effective storyteller using data. Course 2: Excel Basics for Data Analysis At the end of this course, you will have developed a basic working

title: How to Study for the IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate
content: knowledge for using Excel spreadsheets for data analysis. This course covers the basics of working with spreadsheets and their usage in the process of analyzing data. From there, you will learn the fundamentals of data wrangling, cleaning, and analyzing using spreadsheets. Course 3: Data Visualization and Dashboards with Excel and Cognos This course delves further into the features and functions of spreadsheets and leaves you with the ability to complete basic data analyses using Excel and IBM

title: How to Study for the IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate
content: Cognos Analytics without writing any code. Course 4: Python for Data Science, AI, and Development By the end of this course, you will go from zero programming experience to writing Python code in a matter of hours. Course 5: Python Project for Data Science This project course is a chance for you to demonstrate and practice your newfound Python skills for working with data by developing a dashboard using Python. Course 6: Databases and SQL for Data Science with Python This course introduces you

title: How to Study for the IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate
content: to relational database concepts and helps you learn the basics of the SQL language. Topics covered include

title: How to Study for the IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate
content: importing datasets, cleaning data, data frame manipulation, summarizing data, building Machine Learning regression models, and building data pipelines. You will learn how to use popular Python libraries such as Pandas, Numpy, and Scipy to complete these tasks. Course 8: Data Visualization with Python This course teaches you to create effective data visualizations using popular Python libraries including Matplotlib, Seaborn, and Folium. Course 9: IBM Data Analyst Capstone Project This culmination

title: How to Study for the IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate
content: of the program offers you the chance to complete a full data analysis from the beginning of collecting data from multiple sources all the way through to presenting your data analysis report with an executive summary. How much does the certificate cost? The IBM Data Analytics Professional Certificate is accessed through the Coursera online learning platform which has a $39 (USD) monthly subscription fee. Therefore, if you take the suggested 11 months to complete the course, the cost will be

title: How to Study for the IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate
content: approximately $429 (USD). Due to the monthly cost, it may make sense to try to complete the course as quickly as possible to reduce cost. However, it’s important to bear in mind that this course is already considerably more affordable than a data science bootcamp (where you can be paying anywhere between $3,000 to $15,000 for the experience) or if you were to get a Master’s degree in data science. Coursera also provides financial aid and scholarships for those in need. Coursera also provides an

title: How to Study for the IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate
content: option where you can audit a course or the entire program. You won’t receive a certificate or have the ability to submit any assignments and receive grades on them, but you will still be able to access all of the course materials. How to study for the IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate. Despite their accessibility, MOOCs on average have a completion rate of less than 10%. This makes it even more important for you to do your due diligence early on and figure out the best way to complete

title: How to Study for the IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate
content: this certificate. Developing a dedicated study schedule, especially if self-study isn’t really your forte, will help you get through the course and successfully retain everything you learned. IBM suggests that you can complete the course in 11 months if you dedicate 3 hours per week to going through the course material. For your average person with commitments outside of work and a full-time job, this timeline is reasonable. However, this course can be completed in a much shorter timeframe (1–4

title: How to Study for the IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate
content: months) if you have no other commitments. With 100+ hours of course content to get through, it’s impossible to get anything from the course if you’re simply passively watching the videos and not actually getting your hands dirty with taking notes or completing the assignments and practice problems. In other words, to get the most out of the course and actually develop those skills that will make you eligible in a competitive job market, you have to work. Understand the learning process. As

title: How to Study for the IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate
content: mentioned above, MOOCs have an average completion rate of less than 10%, which may arguably be due to a lack of disciplined study on the student’s part. With humans having a shorter attention span than a goldfish, it’s only natural for us to begin something only to be distracted by something shinier and newer that pops up. Knowing this, we need to be smarter, more diligent, and more disciplined about our learning to finish online courses. However, before setting up a schedule, you need to figure

title: How to Study for the IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate
content: out a few things first. It’s easy in the beginning when you’re all gung-ho to say that you will study for ten hours per day and finish the course in less than 3 months. That is until you actually try to study for ten hours per day for a week and realize how hard that is – especially when you haven’t done that since you were in college. If you follow this methodology, you’ll become part of the statistic of 90% of people who don’t finish MOOCs. It’s also important to remember that your brain needs

title: How to Study for the IBM Data Analyst Professional Certificate
content: time to learn things. Those who abide by the 20-hour rule understand that while it only takes 20 hours to become reasonably good at a skill, those 20 hours of study can’t take place over two days and have any discernable returns. This phenomenon has to do with neuroplasticity – otherwise known as the brain’s ability to change and adapt as a result of experience. title: Data Analyst’s Primer to Slowly Changing Dimensions
content: Source: Photo by Tobias Fischer on Unsplash I was presented with a SQL challenge that was relatively straight forward, but included a comment that the columns in the challenge’s hypothetical tables were Slowly Changing Dimensions Type 2. I had no idea what these were but fortunately it was a take home challenge so I had the opportunity to research it and be successful on the challenge and the interview process. Beyond knowing the impact on my coding challenge, I was also curious as to why this

title: Data Analyst’s Primer to Slowly Changing Dimensions
content: would be important to the role of Data Analyst. When I made my career transition by attending a Data Science bootcamp, instructors and peers all said that Google would be your best friend, indicating that solving problems you are presented with require research – not all questions have an easy or straightforward answer. But in this instance, Google was not very helpful. As of 2021, the first result when searching for "slowly changing dimensions" is now a Wikipedia article that did not exist when

title: Data Analyst’s Primer to Slowly Changing Dimensions
content: I was presented with my coding challenge. Instead, the best result I found was an Oracle primer describing the different types of slowly changing dimensions but the remaining results were not very helpful. I turned my attention to searching YouTube and found a a helpful result by a user called Tech Coach that explained slowly changing dimensions in a manner helpful for approaching the interview challenge along with important knowledge applicable in my daily role as a Data Analyst. Below I have

title: Data Analyst’s Primer to Slowly Changing Dimensions
content: summarized the findings of my research along with denoting applications for Data Analysts. My goals with providing these details are: Synthesize my own research findings to help others enhance their knowledge or prepare for an interview Identify situations when slowly changing dimensions might have an impact on your queries Provide background knowledge as to why slowly changing dimensions have relevance to a Data Analyst’s daily work. So what are Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD)? SCDs refer to a

title: Data Analyst’s Primer to Slowly Changing Dimensions
content: data warehousing concept where dimensions contain both current AND historical data. This is a common approach to maintaining historical details in a data warehouse but their use will depend on both the business needs and purpose of the data warehouse. At a basic level, the dimension will change slowly over time rather than at a scheduled interval – there is no fixed pattern in the frequency of the dimension changes. This raises the question as to whether the data warehouse will store current or

title: Data Analyst’s Primer to Slowly Changing Dimensions
content: historical data or both. The decision will likely be dictated by business need and will be implemented and managed by a Data Architect or Engineer, but understanding the type of dimensions used and the rationale will be critical to the Data Analyst’s ability to respond to business questions and perform their role effectively. A business case for using slowly changing dimensions may be when we may need to account for what attributes that we know will change over time but we do not necessarily

title: Data Analyst’s Primer to Slowly Changing Dimensions
content: expect changes at a defined interval. For example, consider a sales department where as the number of accounts changes, individual account executive responsible to specific customers will change. These changes will occur as the company acquires new accounts, but we do not know exactly when this will change as opposed to scheduled promotions and salary changes for employees in the sales department that occur every June. So what are the different types of slowly changing dimensions? SCD Type 0 The

title: Data Analyst’s Primer to Slowly Changing Dimensions
content: first type is referred to as Type 0. This refers to attributes that never change and will not be updated in the data warehouse. An example of SCD Type 0 would be a record we would not expect to ever change such as date of birth or an employee’s start date with a company. As a result, we would not expect this dimension to change in our data warehouse. SCD Type 1 A Slowly Changing Dimension Type 1 refers to an instance where the latest snapshot of a record is maintained in the data warehouse,

title: Data Analyst’s Primer to Slowly Changing Dimensions
content: without any historical records. SCD Type 1 are commonly used to correct errors in a dimension updating values that were wrong or irrelevant. No history is retained – if a record contained errors and required updates, do we want to retain that inaccurate history that is now deprecated? A real world example comes from your author. My first name is Nicolas but human error or tools such as autocorrect often assume that the correct way to spell my name is the more common Nicholas with an h in my

title: Data Analyst’s Primer to Slowly Changing Dimensions
content: name. Suppose this error was made by the HR team when I join a new company. Naturally, I would want the records to reflect my name accurately so HR would change my name in the source system. Any tables in the data warehouse built off of the source system like an employee names and roles table would be updated to reflect this change. A SCD Type 1 would update the record to reflect my name accurately, correcting the error in the name spelling. The incorrect record would be updated without adding

title: Data Analyst’s Primer to Slowly Changing Dimensions
content: any new rows or columns to the data warehouse. However, suppose the record was not an incorrect name but something such as an employment history table – for example, an employee’s role and salary within the company. When an employee gets promoted, a SCD Type 1 record would reflect their new position – the prior record is overwritten. So if we are sure we don’t need the prior history (e.g., correcting a mistake), SCD Type 1 might serve our purposes. But consider the example below: Paulie is a

title: Data Analyst’s Primer to Slowly Changing Dimensions
content: District Sales Manager and is promoted to Regional Sales Manager. Because of his promotion, the employee table in the Data Warehouse would be updated. The prior record and employment history would be overwritten to reflect the new position, salary, supervisor and so on. In SCD Type 1, the employment history would be overwritten. So in the example above, our table would retain the second row – Paulie’s current position as Regional Sales Manager but his prior history as a District Sales

title: Data Analyst’s Primer to Slowly Changing Dimensions
content: Managerwould not be retained in our table. However, there may be valid reasons why we want to retain the history. For example, Human Resources may want to easily access someone’s supervisor or salary history or identify the frequency with which an employee changes roles. In the latter circumstance, SCD Type 1 would not be appropriate because we would lose the history, which leads us to our next type of slowly changing dimensions. SCD Type 2 So what is used when we want to maintain the history?

title: Data Analyst’s Primer to Slowly Changing Dimensions
content: Introducing the Slowly Changing Dimension Type 2. With SCD Type 2, every time there is a change in the source system, a new row will be added to the data warehouse table. In the resulting table, there will be more records, but the prior history is retained and queryable. In SCD Type 2, there would be two methods to distinguish between current and historical records: A column signifying the current record to_date and from_date columns Continuing the example above, consider that Paulie has now

title: Data Analyst’s Primer to Slowly Changing Dimensions
content: been promoted to the Head of East Coast Sales. Since we are now looking at SCD Type 2, all the records from Paulie’s prior roles will be retained in our employee_historytable. The current record in the table will be signified by a flag ( current_record_indicator ) or via the date range where the current record will have standardized surrogate high date (e.g. position_end_date = '12-31-9999' ). When querying the table, to ensure we return current records we would add a filtering condition such

title: Data Analyst’s Primer to Slowly Changing Dimensions
content: as: WHERE current_record = 'Y' or WHERE position_end_date = '12-31-9999' Depending on the structure of the table, the data warehouse and business needs, only one or both columns/methods may be available. To recap SCD Type 2, the main benefit is that the history of a record will be maintained, however, this type is less likely to be used if there is a possibility that the structure of the data will change (e.g., new columns added to the table) or adding new rows to the table adds to the size such

title: Data Analyst’s Primer to Slowly Changing Dimensions
content: that the table will become unmanageable. In my experience, SCD Type 2 has been common and it is important to understand how to obtain the current record of interest. An important consideration is whether there is an impact to join conditions when building a SQL query. When joining to a table with SCD Type 2, it will be important to include the current record flag in your join conditions, failing to do so could skew your results. SCD Type 3 The next type of Slowly Changing Dimensions is Type 3,

title: Data Analyst’s Primer to Slowly Changing Dimensions
content: in my career I have not encountered this situation and my research on the topic indicates that this type is infrequently used. Instead of adding new rows to the table to reflect each record change, an additional column is added. Consider the previous example with Paulie’s promotion from District to Regional Sales Manager. To capture Paulie’s new salary, we added a new row to the table, preserving the prior history. Instead, with SCD Type 3, we would have one row, but an additional column to

title: Data Analyst’s Primer to Slowly Changing Dimensions
content: denote the previous and current salary, along with a date the record was updated: SCD Type 3 This will compare Paulie’s salary from the original and current state, but tracking history will be more difficult if the salary changes again. The advantage to this approach is that it offers the ability to compare a record before and after a change occurred, however limited history is preserved. SCD Type 4 The next slowly changing dimension is Type 4. Here, the concept of a history table is introduced.

title: Data Analyst’s Primer to Slowly Changing Dimensions
content: Historical data will be maintained as in SCD Type 2 but the distinction here is that the history will be maintained on a separate table within the data warehouse. The current record will be included in the primary table. With SCD Type 4, for each change in the source system, a record will be added to the history table. Continuing our example with Paulie and his promotions in the Sales department: Our employee table in the data warehouse would reflect Paulie’s current role as Head of East Coast

title: Data Analyst’s Primer to Slowly Changing Dimensions
content: Sales: employee table (current records) While a separate employee_history table would contain historical data about prior roles Paulie has held with the same company: SCD Type 4 History Table A Human Resources manager interested in Paulie’s salary or job title history could look up prior records in the employee_history table by joining on employee_id. Wrapping Up The above reflects my own research and experience while introducing the applicability of this Data Architecture concept to the Data

title: Data Analyst’s Primer to Slowly Changing Dimensions
content: Analyst role. By no means is this exhaustive and for those really interested in structuring a data warehouse I would encourage further research or seeking the input of a Data Architect.

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: Office Hours Photo by Emily Morter on Unsplash My blog journey continues! Since I will start my MBA journey this August, I will be away from the workplace for 10 months. I definitely want to continue to work in a data-related role afterward, so I’d like to write a summary of what I found really helpful during my first years as a Data Analyst— also for my own record. There are a lot of useful resources on the Internet from which I have learned a lot. Hence, I try my best to keep this post as

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: unique and personal as possible to reduce overlaps. Before I dive into those tips, let me share my definition of a good Data Analyst, i.e., where I wanted to be and have been working towards in the last couple of years. Note that this might be very different from what a specific company or in general the market expects from a Data Analyst. 😃 Back to the end of 2019, I wrote the following New Year’s resolution on my LinkedIn with an amazing view from Cabo da Roca

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/wenling-y-25146887_wordoftheyear-2020resolution-activity-6618244271386447873-bz3D), where I already had a rough idea of what in my view makes a good data person. Those points are still valid: helping stakeholders to ask the right question, telling a good data story, and learning fast. Image by Author In my first blog post, I share some good practices on data storytelling. Here I would like to expand on some other tips. They are: 🧭 Find the "compass" KPIs and use

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: them as benchmarks for quick sanity checks when you generate new insights. This allows for quick learning in a new context. 🔢 Back up yourself with data whenever possible. I mean … there is a word "data" in our titles, right? 😉 ⛳️ Start with the goals. Always. This helps you identify your real value as a data person beyond "writing queries, creating dashboards, and sending spreadsheets". 🙌 Establish your accountability, pivot yourself as an equal, competent, and trustworthy business partner and

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: grow the same accountability from your coworkers. Find your own compass(es) in the ocean of data. During the five years with my current employer, together with my team I have created and shared tons of dashboards and reports, built a company-wide OKR system, created a payback calculator for our board, I could proudly say that I have become one of those who are most familiar with our data. Nevertheless, still every day I feel that I am learning something new about our business because we can

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: always find a new lens through to look into our data. Navigating through this complexity while maintaining our quality standards, i.e., to adapt ourselves into a new context and generate insights for our stakeholders quickly and accurately, is definitely a challenge. One thing that helped me a lot is to keep in mind 5–7 high-level KPIs and always use them as benchmarks for quick sanity checks when I generate some new insights. Photo by Austin Neill on Unsplash How do I decide which KPIs to

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: remember? The AARRR framework provides a good direction: Acquisition: what is the size of our total customer base? How many new customers are acquired each month? Activation: what is the conversion rate of our signup funnel? How many customers sign up at least once per month? Retention: what is the Day1 retention rate of our app (%)? Referral: how many customers (%) are acquired through our referral program? How many customers (%) recommend their families & friends to use our product? Revenue:

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: how many customers (%) have generated revenue for our business? What is the average of our monthly revenue in the last 12 months? Note that we don’t have to remember the very accurate figures but the orders of the magnitude. Depending on the size of your business, for an absolute number, we may only need to recall if it is 10K, 50K, 100K, or 1M and for a percentage 10%, 50%, or 90%. Does this sound familiar to you? Yes, this is one application of Fermi Estimate! The last reminder: in a rapidly

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: growing business, these numbers would need to be refreshed regularly. 🙂 Why is this helpful? Imagine now I am working on an urgent ad-hoc request. I wrote a query to look at a customer segment I have never looked at before. The query output suggests that 70% of this segment generated revenue. Hold on – I remember that this ratio should be roughly 15% across the whole customer base. 70% vs 15%… that sounds too good to be true! Immediately I suspect that something is off with my query and I

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: quickly figure out that I missed a WHERE clause. Phew! That 15% in my mind helped me with a quick sanity check and saved us from a potentially inaccurate deliverable. This is why I call these figures "compass(es)" – I may not bear in mind the exact coordinates while traveling over the sea, but as long as I know where is the south I can always quickly find my way out. Back up yourself with data whenever possible. There is a word "Data" in my title and I know what it makes others expect from me.

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: Even when I do not deliver any data or insights, I always make sure my arguments are backed up by data whenever possible. The word "data" here does not necessarily mean that you have to know the exact figures or mathematical formula. It is more about specifying what data you would look at and how you would use them to support your arguments and make better decisions. Photo by Franki Chamaki on Unsplash I want to use one interview question as an example to explain how this works. During one

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: interview I was asked how I would help assess the effectiveness of a catalog campaign. First of all, I started by defining the success metric as the conversion rate of the campaign, i.e., out of those who receive the catalogs how many make purchases afterward. Then the interviewer asked me, "Sounds great. How would you determine which purchases are triggered by the catalogs?" – This is essentially the tracking and collection of data. I proposed we embed a promotional code in the catalog for

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: users to enter during checkout and use this code to identify purchases from catalog recipients. The interviewer nodded, and chased with another question, "what if some users don’t use the promotional code?" I answered, "we can apply an attribution window, that is, we attribute all purchases from the recipients within X days after the catalogs are sent as purchases from that campaign" – This is where human logic kicks in to cover the limitations of data tracking. The interviewer agreed to that

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: proposal, and asked the final question, "how would you determine X?". I said, "I would look at historical data of similar campaigns for a benchmark. If I see that 90% of purchases from these recipients were made within 14 days after the catalogs are sent, then I would take 14 days as the attribution window because with that I can cover at least 90% conversions. If no historical data is available, I would design a small-scale experiment to collect that data." I really enjoyed this interview

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: question not because I scored all points, but because it was going so natural as a conversation with my coworkers in daily life and it covered a simple flow of using data to support decision making. No complex calculation is required at all. 🙂 Start with the goals. Always. When I started as a junior data analyst, I viewed my top priority as delivering exactly what people ask of me. If someone came to me and asked for a monthly sales report, I made sure I deliver the accurate figures – not

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: monthly customer figures, not daily sales trends, but exactly the amount of sales we closed in each month. It did not take long before I got the impression that this may not be the best work mode. Sometimes people ask for a monthly sales report, I deliver it and both of us are happy. However, the next day they come to me again and ask "Hey, actually I need this report to design a new bonus scheme for our sales agents. Can we break it down by agent name?" For sure! But wouldn’t it be even better

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: if I can have a good understanding of my colleague’s goal beforehand so that we can together come up with a better solution on our first try? Sometimes I also get requests that do not make full sense in their original forms. For this, I can share an even more concrete example. In our current setup, my team is responsible for helping Product Managers set up success metrics and data tracking for their features. One day a PM came to me and asked me to implement a backend event that is triggered

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: when a certain document is SENT to a user. The first check I did together with him is to see what KPIs he was looking to measure with the tracking. It turned out that he wanted to see out of those users who SEE the document in their accounts, how many would take a certain action. Then I explained to him that we actually already have a frontend event in a place that tracks users’ view on that document and that the new backend event he suggested is not necessary and it won’t help measure the KPI

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: he wants to look at (as it tracks the SEND action rather than VIEW action). My colleague eventually took my suggestion. By doing so, I actually did not deliver the thing that my stakeholder asked me to do, but did I deliver any value? I think yes! I helped my colleague clarify a myth around the KPI definition and save us one task that would cost engineering capacity – we have really severe resource constraint on this matter just like every startup 🙂 Photo by Munkhtuvshin .T on Unsplash My

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: takeaway from this example is that as a data person (be it data analyst, data scientist, data product manager… all those data-related non-engineering roles seem to have increasingly blurry boundaries these days), sometimes you create value for your coworkers and your business not by executing exactly their wishes but by helping them achieve their ultimate goals. This starts by figuring together with them what their goals really are instead of taking their requirements as they are presented in

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: the first place. Actually, I will quote one of my supervisors, "The difference between junior data analysts and senior data analysts is that: juniors always do what they are told to do yet seniors don’t." One last bonus point on this topic: understanding the goal of your stakeholders, that is, how the data or insights you deliver will help them make their decisions and what kind of decisions they are, definitely helps you understand your real value as a data person and boost your confidence.

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: Your real value is not demonstrated by how many dashboards or analyses you have delivered, but by the impacts on business outcomes and user experiences that are inspired and driven by your deliverables. Establish your accountability as a trusted business partner. We’ve and seen heard the word "Stakeholder Management" in many places – actually, so many that to be honest, I start to get a bit fed up with it. 😅 There are many great pieces of content on the internet about this area, so here I just

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: want to share two things that I found really useful in earning the trust of my stakeholders as a data person. In my first blog post How I do Data Storytelling, I mentioned one tip "Know your data through and through" as one way to maintain people’s trust in the data, the two things I shared here would be a little more generic and can be transferable to other professions as well. One thing is to keep your main stakeholders well informed about the major milestones and blockers while working on

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: rather big analyses or projects. "Big analyses" refers to the type of analyses that usually have: 1) explorative and open-end research questions, 2) high uncertainty about the quality of source data and thus deliverables (Remember – Garbage in, garbage out 😉 ), and 3) a rather long timeline for delivery (e.g., >1 week). What I usually do in this case is to schedule 2–3 touchpoints along the timeline with my stakeholders where I give a brief description of where we stand, what we have achieved,

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: and what is blocking us. It does not have to be a meeting – a short email can do the job as well. The goal of this touchpoint is not to simply let people know "hey we are doing our job", but to seek instant feedback about our methodology and delivery as well as to seek support when we are stuck. By doing so, not only my stakeholders but also myself would have more transparency into the delivery, more flexibility to adapt the scope, more valuable feedback for improvements, and more support if we

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: just ask for it! In the end, together we will make better-informed decisions. Another thing that I found valuable is to always close the loop. Every day we deliver new insights and data, sparkling exchanges take place, new ideas and feedback come to our tables. In a rapidly changing workplace, it is very easy to lose traces and end up with an unresolved backlog – that makes me feel unachieved. Hence, most of the time I make sure I get feedback or acknowledgment for my deliverables (at least for

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: those with high-level goals behind them). If I deliver any insights or data, more than sending over an excel sheet or PDF, I would always invite for feedback (e.g., "let us know if you still have any questions"), and I would not consider a task as resolved until I get a confirmative "yes, we don’t have any questions for now". This helps me keep a maintainable backlog as I know there is hardly any debt but just more new ideas to be explored. Eventually, this contributes to the efficiency and

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: reliability of my work mode, as I don’t have to worry that one day some unresolved task would pop up like a mine and block other deliveries. Photo by Windows on Unsplash In fact, this is not only about establishing my own image as an equal, competent, and trustworthy business partner but also about growing the same accountability from my coworkers. This process is definitely not easy, but I believe in the end this helps foster a strong trust and bond between me and my coworkers (at least those

title: What helped me become a better Data Analyst
content: who share the same goal). That’s it! As always, let me know if you find this useful or share any feedback!

title: Awesome AWS-Quicksight Visuals Every Data Analyst Should Know
content: Almost everyone who analyses data for a living uses one visualization tool or another. There are hundreds of tools for visualizing data. Be it in the Python programming environment with packages like Matplotlib, Plotly, and Bokeh or with built-up software like SAP Lumira, Tableau, or even Excel, we have more tools at our disposal than we can possibly ever use. How do you choose the best then? Well, actually almost all of them are pretty good implementations. Your choice depends on your use case.

title: Awesome AWS-Quicksight Visuals Every Data Analyst Should Know
content: I have used Tableau for most use cases until now because of the ease of sharing dashboards on a server for the end-users to use. But it lacks in capabilities when we need to create certain types of visuals. For example, you would have to go through a tedious ritual to create even simple flow diagrams. And good luck remembering all the aggregations and data multiplications at the end of it. Plotly certainly helps in such cases but then you have to bear the pain of creating a good data framework

title: Awesome AWS-Quicksight Visuals Every Data Analyst Should Know
content: from scratch for every visual that is needed. A tool that I recently came across eliminates several of the above limitations. It combines the best of many visualization software into a cloud-based Business Intelligence Service. It is called Quicksight and it is offered as a service within Amazon Web Services (AWS). You can read more in the documentation here: Amazon QuickSight – Business Intelligence Service – Amazon Web Services After a few days working on Quicksight, I found several

title: Awesome AWS-Quicksight Visuals Every Data Analyst Should Know
content: visualizations there that are offered as standard, which would otherwise take ages to build in other tools. For anyone new to AWS and Quicksight, there is ample documentation available. If you like, you can quickly go through an overview of how to connect your data in Quicksight, before we get into the visuals: Creating Datasets Using New Data Sources – Amazon QuickSight In this article, I will take you through 7 visuals that I absolutely liked using in Quicksight, in a countdown to my most

title: Awesome AWS-Quicksight Visuals Every Data Analyst Should Know
content: favorite. Why do I like them? Because of: The simplicity involved in data preparation Intuitiveness offered to the end-user Frequency of use (based on my use cases) I’ll take you through the basic data structure required along with the resulting visual. With the knowledge and combination of these visuals, you can create spellbinding dashboards too! 7. Waterfall Charts Waterfall charts are used when we need to show a cumulative increase or decrease in values over a period of time. Though many

title: Awesome AWS-Quicksight Visuals Every Data Analyst Should Know
content: tools out there can create these charts, Quicksight offers the simplest one. Consider the following cumulative data of a company’s revenue and expenses: Screenshot by the Author All you need to do is import the Excel data in Quicksight. Once the data is imported, select the Waterfall Chart from the Visual Type selection area in the bottom left corner. You will see a blank area for a chart and a section called Field Wells above it. The Field Wells required for creating a Waterfall Chart are:

title: Awesome AWS-Quicksight Visuals Every Data Analyst Should Know
content: Category Value Breakdown (optional) Drag the Type and Value columns from the Field List into Category and Value in the Field Wells __ respectively. And there you go, the chart is ready! Screenshot by the Author 6. Funnel Chart A funnel chart is basically used to show the flow through any business process, most commonly in sales. For. e.g., with the help of these charts, we can see the drop in the count of users in each step of the process (which gives the characteristic funnel shape). Consider

title: Awesome AWS-Quicksight Visuals Every Data Analyst Should Know
content: the following cumulative data of book sales process, from the estimated market size to the total copies sold: Screenshot by the Author Once you import the data into Quicksight, select the Funnel Chart from the Visual Types section. The Field Wells required are: Group by Value Drag the Book Sales and Count columns from the Field List into Category and Value in the Field Wells. Screenshot by the Author 5. Tree Map After the 2 simple charts that we went through till now, let’s go towards more

title: Awesome AWS-Quicksight Visuals Every Data Analyst Should Know
content: complex and fun charts. One such visual type is a Tree Map, one of my go-to charts in several use cases. It is used to represent hierarchical data in the form of nested rectangles. The nodes in this type of chart are categorized with two dimensions of size and color, giving us a very compact and data-rich visualization. Consider the following dummy data consisting of product items, their quantity, and total price: Screenshot by the Author Select the Tree Map from the Visual Types section after

title: Awesome AWS-Quicksight Visuals Every Data Analyst Should Know
content: the data import. The Field Wells required are: Group by Size Colour Drag the Item, Quantity, and Price columns from the Field List into Group by, Size and Colour in the Field Wells respectively. Screenshot by the Author As you see, each tile in the diagram quantifies a given item in the data based on quantity and price represented with size and the color of the tile respectively. This makes it a very handy visual type when the classification involves two dimensions. 4. Heat Map It is a Data

title: Awesome AWS-Quicksight Visuals Every Data Analyst Should Know
content: Visualization technique that shows the magnitude of an event as color. Usually, the variation in color intensity is used to give obvious visual cues to the end-user about how the event is clustered. Hence, one of the common uses of a Heat Map is to visualize natural environmental phenomenon. Additionally, it is used to visualize fluid flow dynamics, surface distortions, etc. With that in mind, what is better data to visualize as a Heat map than the temperature data of a city? In this case, I

title: Awesome AWS-Quicksight Visuals Every Data Analyst Should Know
content: downloaded the weather data for Berlin from here and did a bit of data engineering to get the Dates, Hour of Day, and the Temperature (in degrees Celcius). So the final data for import in Quicksight looks like this: Screenshot by the Author Select the Heat Map from the Visual Types section after the data import. The field wells required are: Rows Columns Values Drag the Date, Hour of Day, and Temperature columns from the Field List into Rows, Columns, and Values in the Field Wells respectively.

title: Awesome AWS-Quicksight Visuals Every Data Analyst Should Know
content: Screenshot by the Author Voila! An amazing Heat map in a matter of seconds. This is definitely one of my favorite visualization types, but there is more to come. 3. Points On Map This is a pretty ubiquitous visualization nowadays. It is used to visualize populations of countries, pandemic outbreaks, air traffic routes, supply chains, and the list goes on. It is very likely that no matter in which industry you work, you will probably use or see this visual type in your company dashboard. Hence it

title: Awesome AWS-Quicksight Visuals Every Data Analyst Should Know
content: is only practical to have this as a standard visual type. In Quicksight, this implementation is called Points on Map, and it understands data based on latitude, longitude, city names, or even the zip-codes! (though you may have to wait for its availability based on your geography, it only just became available in Europe). To demonstrate how it works, I use the population data from the German Cities Database I found here. Screenshot by the Author Once you import the data, select the Points on Map

title: Awesome AWS-Quicksight Visuals Every Data Analyst Should Know
content: from the Visual Types section. The field wells required are: Geospatial (latitude, longitude, city name, etc.) Size Colour Drag the lat & lng columns from the Field List into Geospatial, and Population in the Size **** Field Well. You can also use the color in case there is another parameter to be indicated for e.g. population density. Screenshot by the Author And there you have it. It is that easy to have an amazing map visualization! 2. Word Cloud Word Cloud is used as a visual representation

title: Awesome AWS-Quicksight Visuals Every Data Analyst Should Know
content: of text data that may or may not in any particular sequence or order. Is also a chart that became very common with the rise of social media and text analytics fields. They are particularly popular to give an intuitive representation of word frequencies used, for e.g. hashtags, keywords or even analyzing texts from web pages or books. There are many online tools available to build word clouds for free. But such an implementation in the AWS environment is what makes it powerful. You can analyze

title: Awesome AWS-Quicksight Visuals Every Data Analyst Should Know
content: data using python and create an output dataset for import in Quicksight. This opens up a wide range of possibilities for highly flexible text visualizations! To demonstrate here, I created a dummy dataset of a list of members from a survey and their native languages: Once you import the data, select the Word Cloud from the Visual Types section. The field wells required are: Group by Size Drag the Native Language column from the Field List into Group by. It will automatically generate the cloud

title: Awesome AWS-Quicksight Visuals Every Data Analyst Should Know
content: based on the count! You can also use the size indicator, in case your data is structured differently with word counts in a different column. The only thing I miss is the absence of a color field, to show different words in different colors. It would make the visualization all the more appealing (I really hope this gets implemented in a future update). Screenshot by the Author 1. Sankey Diagram And finally, to the visual type that I enjoy using the most because of its flexibility and

title: Awesome AWS-Quicksight Visuals Every Data Analyst Should Know
content: intuitiveness. Sankey diagrams are in essence flow diagrams in which the flow paths indicate a proportionality to the quantity flowing (or rate, or any other measure in the flow). This makes a Sankey diagram an absolute treasure in use cases such as energy flows, material flows, networks, process chains in business operations, and so on. The only hurdle in their lack of ubiquity until now was an absence of a simple implementation. We can do it in Tableau, but only with a thousand circuitous

title: Awesome AWS-Quicksight Visuals Every Data Analyst Should Know
content: methods. Or we can code such ourselves. All this can be avoided by the simplest ever implementation I have found to date in Business Intelligence software. Consider the data below (derived from Germany’s Energy Flow Chart – 2018, that I found here): Screenshot by the Author All you need is a source, destination, and a flow quantity between both. Let us see how this works. Once you import the data, select the Sankey Diagram from the Visual Types section. The field wells required are: Source

title: Awesome AWS-Quicksight Visuals Every Data Analyst Should Know
content: Destination Weight Drag the Source, Destination, and Units (Petajoules) columns from the Field List into Source, Destination, and Weight in the Field Wells respectively. In seconds, you have magic! A visual representation of the flows based on the data. The implementation automatically adjusts itself according to the quantities given, which means any error in the values will make the diagram look a bit awkward (for example if more is flowing out than in). Screenshot by the Author The simplicity

title: Awesome AWS-Quicksight Visuals Every Data Analyst Should Know
content: of its implementation makes it the best visualization rated on this list! That was the list of 7 visual types in AWS Quicksight! With a combination of these and many more that are offered and continuously upgrades, I am sure you can already be on your way to being an amazing visual storyteller! Which ones did you like? Is it just me or do you also have a few go-to visualization types that you use often? I would definitely like to know and learn more. Feel free to let me know in the comments!

title: How to Onboard New Data Analysts
content: Have you ever started at a new company and the onboarding process was less than optimal? Your manager didn’t have a clear idea where you should begin and onboarding meant learning as you went along. After working as a data scientist and then a data analyst this is what I’ve found helped me onboard faster and add value even when I didn’t have clear guidance. Understand the company business My first onboarding item was to understand the company business model, primary sources of revenue, and KPIs

title: How to Onboard New Data Analysts
content: used to measure success. This knowledge helped me during A/B test discussions on experiment design and decide on KPIs to measure success. I was also able to prioritize requests based on impact to KPIs affecting revenue and justify to stakeholders why other requests were deprioritized. Learn the data My next item was learning what data was in the database. I reviewed tables, field values, and ETL jobs to help me understand the join logic between tables and business logic applied to calculate KPI

title: How to Onboard New Data Analysts
content: values. I also reviewed available data dictionaries and lookup tables to understand field values specific to the company such as product identifiers and pricing codes. Learning the data early on helped in multiple ways when I met with stakeholders to discuss requests. First, I was able to respond immediately if a request was possible based on data availability instead of researching after the fact and getting back to the stakeholder. Second, I could present alternatives using other data sources

title: How to Onboard New Data Analysts
content: and conclude the requirements discussion in the same meeting instead of having a second meeting because I didn’t know the answer offhand. Meet and greet Set up 30-minute meet and greet meetings with people you’re likely to interact within the company. If you’re not sure who to talk to ask your manager or stakeholders for a list of people they recommend you meet. I found this was a great way to break the ice with people in a new company and know who to ask if I had a question about a specific

title: How to Onboard New Data Analysts
content: issue. With many people currently working remotely, this is one item where it’s even more beneficial for new data analysts to do during their onboarding process. I didn’t talk to all my stakeholders during the interview process and these meetings helped me understand their role in the company and what insights I could provide to help them meet their goals. Don’t accept the status quo As a new data analyst, you come in with fresh eyes and can identify issues where existing employees may not see

title: How to Onboard New Data Analysts
content: any. Just because the company has always done things a certain way doesn’t mean there’s no room for improvement. Ask questions about pain points your stakeholders or colleagues are experiencing and identify any areas that can be improved. When I first started as a data analyst at my current company, the ETL that updated the subscriptions dashboard was split into 4 jobs and was inefficient to rerun if the job failed because I had to manually rerun the jobs one after the other. This caused a

title: How to Onboard New Data Analysts
content: reporting delay to stakeholders if any of the jobs failed – which it did often. I rewrote the ETL into 1 job that reduced the runtime to update the dashboard and made my life easier because I only had to manually rerun 1 job instead of 4 if there were failures. Conclusion As a data analyst in a new company, it’s not always clear where you should start. For the lucky ones that have an onboarding plan, I congratulate you on having a clear path. For those like me that had to find their way, I hope

title: How to Onboard New Data Analysts
content: these tips will help make your onboarding process easier in the future. You might also like… How to Be a More Productive Data Analyst 4 Habits of Bad Data Analysts

title: Google vs IBM vs Microsoft: Which Online Data Analyst Certificate is Best?
content: How to choose a data analyst certification. When looking into the world of data analyst certifications, it’s important to consider two things when picking your program of choice. Pick the certification with the technologies that most interest you. First, none of the certifications listed above are heads above the rest or even each other. Inherently, the programs listed above are the same, just using different technologies. For instance, each certification has you using technologies specific to

title: Google vs IBM vs Microsoft: Which Online Data Analyst Certificate is Best?

IBM teaches their certification using the Watson platform because everything at IBM runs on Watson. Finally, Microsoft teaches their certification using Microsoft technologies because their whole company uses Microsoft technologies. Once you learn specific technologies and become comfortable with them, you’re less likely to learn something else. In that way, by completing a certification from

title: Google vs IBM vs Microsoft: Which Online Data Analyst Certificate is Best?
content: one of these companies, they are drawing you into using their products religiously. In other words, these certifications double as marketing tools. Therefore, in many ways, it doesn’t matter which company’s certification you choose to complete – choose the one with the technologies that interest you the most because you’re going to learn the same fundamentals regardless of the course you take. Remember that certifications are not golden tickets to employment – pick a certification that gives you

title: Google vs IBM vs Microsoft: Which Online Data Analyst Certificate is Best?
content: practical experience. Second, while companies like Google have publicly made it their mission to help graduates gain employment after completion of their certification (through the Google employer consortium), not all hiring managers outside of this consortium are convinced about the weight of online data analytics certificates. In fact, many don’t often lend much weight to the completion of MOOCs or online professional certifications. Instead, employers tend to look for candidates with work

While the completion of MOOCs is a good indication of commitment towards personal development, MOOCs aren’t the golden ticket to getting a job. Therefore, it’s important to pair your certification of choice with personal projects and work experience to show that you can apply your skills to solve real-world problems. This is where the Google data analyst certification becomes particularly valuable because they offer a capstone project

content: at the end of the course. Completing this capstone project helps get you well on your way to demonstrating that you can apply technical skills to real data problems. Which professional data analyst certification is best? Depending on who you ask, everyone will have a different opinion on which data analyst certification is best. However, based on the (attempted) most unbiased criteria and a general analysis of the curriculums, this investigation concludes that the best professional data analyst

Making such a bold claim ties Google to this promise. Google is well poised to fulfill this claim by having resources in place to support graduates through the whole job preparation process, including a resume-building tool, mock

content: interviews, career networking events, and a consortium of employers who will hire graduates of the program. Google teaches this certificate in R, a Programming language that has a notoriously difficult learning curve. Learning this language with help from instructors and a community will make the process smoother than having to learn it by yourself. From there, graduates can easily teach themselves Python, a language that is very easy to pick up. In this way, learning the hard things first is

content: beneficial and makes you a more well-rounded data analyst who can jump in at any company. Google has decided to provide the opportunity for a capstone project at the end of the program. content: As a data analyst, I’m often faced with a long list of requests and limited time to work on them because I’m either in a meeting, fielding questions from stakeholders, or troubleshooting an ETL problem. Create a list of required information for requests Stakeholders may not put in all the necessary details into a request and

title: How to Be a More Productive Data Analyst
content: analysts will need to clarify the requirements. This wastes time for both parties to discuss requests that could’ve been saved by agreeing on a list of required information beforehand for common requests. Ever since I created a list of required information with stakeholders, I no longer have to track down missing details and can use that time to work

title: How to Be a More Productive Data Analyst
content: on the request instead. Save common queries and links to documentation I save SQL and Python code snippets to avoid writing similar code again for different requests. The more sample code I have to reference the less time I spend having to write code from scratch and that’s helped boost my Productivity. I bookmark links to documentation I reference often to save me from having to search again. This has proven to be a time saver because I can find what I need quickly and go back to the task at

title: How to Be a More Productive Data Analyst
content: hand. Learn to decline meetings If a meeting is informational and your input isn’t needed confirm with the meeting organizer if your attendance is required. You may want to attend to hear more about the subject matter but often times there is a deck or documentation available for review that will give you the same information without having to attend the meeting. Alternatively have the meeting organizer record the meeting and watch the video when you have time. Save the hour you would’ve spent

title: How to Be a More Productive Data Analyst
content: in a meeting and work on a request instead. Turn off instant messaging notifications I work in a Technology company and Slack is our main source of communication to get quick answers to questions. If I’m working on a request that requires my full concentration I turn off Slack notifications for a couple of hours and check my messages when I reach a good stopping point. This has helped my productivity immensely. Schedule

content: back-to-back meetings I know having continuous meetings can be draining but if you have a choice between two one hour meetings with a 30 minute gap in between or two meetings back-to-back I recommend the latter. Try a meeting free day If your calendar has days where you don’t have many recurring meetings consider making that a meeting free day and

title: How to Be a More Productive Data Analyst
content: shift the meetings to other days of the week. If a meeting free day is not possible try blocking time to have a meeting free afternoon. title: Data Analyst vs. Data Scientist
content: Stylised as the sexiest job of the 21st century, data science has emerged as one of the most in-demand professions of recent years – taking hold with a hype that normally only surrounds celebrities. Companies worldwide put lucrative salaries, prestige and the privilege of wielding influence up for grabs to attract analytical talent. Behind all the hype is a growing importance of digital data that’s currently transforming the way we live and work. It’s no wonder that more and more enthusiasts

content: want to break into this new field. But before venturing into data science and analytics with one’s eyes closed, aspirants are well advised to inform themselves about available routes first. Pursuing this train of thought further, one

title: Data Analyst vs. Data Scientist
content: question naturally always arises. What exactly distinguishes the titles of data scientist and Data Analyst? After all, both professions seem to be tasked with extracting business value from data. The logic savvy reader perhaps already knows that sharing similarities doesn’t imply interchangeability. One could complement the other, as both work in unison towards achieving a common goal. Many phenomena out there in the wild share resemblances in some areas and differ starkly in others. The

title: Data Analyst vs. Data Scientist
content: objective of this article is to find an answer to that question of difference. Not only from the perspective of theory, but also from the lens of a seasoned professional who’s seen how data teams function in the real world. This is because it’s no secret that job titles and their fancy echo are one thing, while the reality of day to day workload an entirely different thing. Having said that, let’s look into the common features of the two roles before we explore the aspects in which they differ.

title: Data Analyst vs. Data Scientist
content: Similarities – Data Analysts vs. Data Scientists In fact, by affirming the few aspects which they share and outlining where they diverge, we get closer to grasping both roles better. That, in practice, means that they should always be found working in the same business units, unless the analysts are bound to specific project teams as part of squads in agile frameworks. Quite logical, right? Both use data in the service of business goals, and both need expertise in traditional statistics. There also is this quadrant of

title: Data Analyst vs. Data Scientist
content: communication that they mutually share: conveying useful insights to business leaders by means of data stories, or creating intuitive tools which bring about ‘data-driven’ decision making. Without much contemplation, it’s thus easy to understand that data scientists and data analysts are only worthwhile having inasmuch as they can prove their work as useful. title: Data Analyst vs. Data Scientist
content: jobs. Be that as it may, can we find more similarities by interrogating the ever-wise world wide web? title: Data Analyst vs. Data Scientist

title: Data Analyst vs. Data Scientist
content: experience leveraging that data. Data Analyst – Job Descriptions At any rate, we shall now turn to the details that separate. What they are preoccupied with for the most part

The last point illustrates why reporting routines with visualisation tools such as Tableau are as pivotal as pivoted tables. Data modelling on the other hand is often limited to basic supervised learning or its stats equivalent: regression analysis. From experience, I can also say that novice practitioners

title: Data Analyst vs. Data Scientist
content: sometimes forget that the stage of supplying recommendations is invariably the most important one. That is why it’s so important that analysts learn how to excavate insights which can be acted upon, presentable in both visually compelling and digestible formats. Analysts are tech savvy investigative reporters who make insights accessible. Data Scientist – Job Descriptions Turning now to a similar

title: Data Analyst vs. Data Scientist
content: example of a typical data scientist role from Indeed, we’ll explore some of the key differences. The first noticeable one is the length of the ‘must have’ and role responsibility sections. But is there substance behind the hype or is data science merely a modern myth? Example data scientist job advert. Photo by author. To be

title: Data Analyst vs. Data Scientist
content: fair, data scientists are for that reason expected to be more than analytical wizards. They are supposed to be builders who employ advanced programming to create pipelines that predict and recommend in production environments with near perfect accuracy. Compared with analysts, who’re like investigative reporters, they are a lot more product development than consulting oriented. Although it’s also required of a data scientist to provide data-led commercial advice. Some say the title was coined to

title: Data Analyst vs. Data Scientist
content: manifest that the role was a confluence of three fields: maths/statistics, computer science and domain expertise. And the following quote is said to best encapsulate that: "A data scientist is someone who is better at statistics than any software engineer, and better at software engineering than any statistician." Differences – Data Analysts vs. Data Scientists Greater volumes of data mean stakes are higher: and so are expectations, too. For unlike analysts, who would on average be given

title: Data Analyst vs. Data Scientist
content: spreadsheets with 500 thousand rows and 50 columns to make sense of on their first day, data scientists will likely see the keys to terabytes of data with tens of thousands of columns handed over to them on day one. Everyone would then expect them to magically summon the gems of insight and wisdom out of those volumes of data. Left to their own devices, they will be expected to ingest, transform, explore and model enormous volumes of messy and unstructured data. As some witty writers on medium

title: Data Analyst vs. Data Scientist
content: have said: "Data scientist is a title that conjures up almost mystical abilities of a person garnering insights from deep data lakes with ease, someone who has supernatural hands for data like a 21st century Houdini!" While data analysts mainly work with SQL dialects to paste manageable chunks of data into

title: Data Analyst vs. Data Scientist
content: spreadsheets and programming interfaces like R Studio and Jupyter Notebooks, data scientists are expected to be comfortable with working in cloud computing settings (AWS, Databricks, Hadoop, etc.). There they ingest, process and model volumes of data whose magnitude is often referred to as big data. In view of that, it’s easy to see why data science jobs add those ridiculously long lists of tech-stack requirements. New hires in larger organisations inevitably inherit heaps of sometimes

title: Data Analyst vs. Data Scientist
content: undocumented legacy scripts and custom algorithms that they either need to replace or maintain. With that in mind, it’s no wonder that advanced programming skills are a must-have, where it is only a good to have in most entry-level data analyst positions. For as we’ve discovered in our long exposition of the differences, Data Analyst Jobs are in actual fact less coding intensive, which reveals a rather more subtle point. The

title: Data Analyst vs. Data Scientist
content: careful observer of the tech world would confirm that technical complexity almost always comes with barriers. They create voids between decision making stakeholders and hands-on engineers and scientists. That, in turn, is the space which product managers fill to bridge the gap in communication. And since data science work is commonly surrounded by a fog of mystery, ordinary employees of a firm tend to prefer to reach out to analysts for help. It’s a phenomenon I’ve frequently noticed in the

title: Data Analyst vs. Data Scientist
content: world of business: data scientists tend to be more siloed. Data analysts, on the other hand, tend to be more involved and engaged with other business units, readily helping with issues such as fixing Excel spreadsheets, aiding client pitches with analytical teasers and contributing to overall business performance with dashboards. So, if the reader of this article is more of a consultant who likes to make a difference in the micro context, an analyst position would infinitely be more fulfilling.

title: Data Analyst vs. Data Scientist

Data Analysts vs. Data Scientists – Conclusion All things considered, we’ve explored how the professions of data scientist and data analyst compare and contrast. Sure, we anticipated differences.

title: Data Analyst vs. Data Scientist
content: But surprisingly, we’ve also come to appreciate how similar the two kindred professions actually are. In essence, they both seek to retrieve insights from datasets. content: There are so many articles and social media posts out there attempting to define the difference between data analyst and data scientist roles, a goal that I’ve never quite understood.
