Each row/column represents a neuron, and the intersections between rows/columns represents a color-coded connection weight. The second thing you should notice is that we have a diagonally symmetric matrix. This is to be expected, as

title: Hopfield Networks: Neural Memory Machines
content: the colored intersections between rows/columns are representing weights of symmetric and bi-directional connections that we discussed previously. Technically, we only need one half of this square, but a symmetric array like the one above is easier to calculate and implement in a computer, and it’s much more fun to look at. We now know that the weights of the network’s connections are what determine its attractor dynamics. So the million dollar question is: how do we engineer these weights so

title: Hopfield Networks: Neural Memory Machines
content: that the network has an attractor for each memory we desire it to remember? There are several learning algorithms known to be useful for HNs, but here we’ll be utilizing hebbian learning. The hebbian learning algorithm originates as a rule to describe the phenomenon of synaptic plasticity in biological neural networks. Taken generally, hebbian learning can be condensed to the statement that ‘neurons which fire together, wire together’. In other words, if two neurons which are connected via

title: Hopfield Networks: Neural Memory Machines
content: synapse are active at the same time, their connection strength increases (in the case of HNs, more positive), and their activity becomes more correlated over time. The opposite is true for neurons which fire asynchronously, and instead their connection weights decrease (in the case of HNs, become more negative). In our example of stored images, the intuition behind Hebbian learning is clear. We want the weight between neurons which are either simultaneously ‘lit’ or ‘unlit’, in the target

title: Hopfield Networks: Neural Memory Machines
content: pattern to encourage the alignment of their activity as the network is updated. We also want cells whose states oppose each other to have the opposite behavior. The formula to calculate a single weight between two neurons, i and j, according to hebbian learning is given by: Equation 3 : The Hebbian formula to compute the desired weight between two neurons, neurons i and j (image by author) Where si and sj are the respective states that the neurons i and j will take on in the target pattern. To

title: Hopfield Networks: Neural Memory Machines
content: compute weights which result in several simultaneously-stored patterns, the formula is expanded…: Equation 4 : An expanded version of the Hebbian rule which computes all desired weights for a given pattern, or set of patterns, simultaneously (image by author) …which effectively takes the average computed weight across patterns, where p represents any pattern and n the number of patterns. On the right side, we have the equivalent expression in matrix form, where Y is a matrix containing our

title: Hopfield Networks: Neural Memory Machines
content: patterns as row vectors. Importantly, when storing multiple patterns, the number of bits in each pattern must remain consistent when the network is learning via this algorithm. As previously mentioned, one significant feature of learning in this way is that it is ‘one-shot’, meaning that the network requires only one ‘exposure’ to learn. This is because we compute the entirety of the weights matrix in one operation. One-shot learning is somewhat unique in that it directly contrasts modern deep

title: Hopfield Networks: Neural Memory Machines
content: learning via backpropagation; a process characterized by iteratively adjusting network weights to reduce an error signal. Depending on the task, training via backpropagation often requires tens of thousands, or even millions, of training examples. This makes it a poor candidate as a model for human episodic memory processing which, by definition, requires one ‘episode’ for memorization. Interestingly, the hippocampus, an area known to have attractor-like dynamics, is actively recruited during

title: Hopfield Networks: Neural Memory Machines
content: one-shot learning, and sparse ensembles in this area are known to coordinate the recapitulation of past-cortical states during episodic memory recall. It’s beyond interesting to me that functional and architectural symmetries exist between what have been observed in biological networks in-vivo, and the behavior of attractor networks in-silico. To me, this suggests that the underlying mechanisms behind such behaviors as memory, cognition, and learning, may be more ‘fundamental’ than the systems

content: by which they’re physically instantiated, whether it be the brain or CPU, etc… Up to now we’ve covered HN structure, behavior, and learning. Next, we tie everything together and understand why HNs behave the way they do using the notion of network energy. We know that regardless of the initial state of an HN, it trends toward a ‘fixed-point’ attractor in state-space. ‘Fixed point’ is one way of describing that the network state remains steady, i.e. the network could update forever at this point

title: Hopfield Networks: Neural Memory Machines
content: and no neurons would flip. This phenomenon is not foreign to us; we commonly observe systems which converge to steady states. Consider a ball rolling down a hill until it sits at the bottom, or a dropped coin spinning rapidly on the ground until it rests stationary on one of its sides. The states of such systems, which you could describe as the objects’ positions, velocities, etc, converge to configurations which do not change without further perturbation. Using the Ising model as an example,

title: Hopfield Networks: Neural Memory Machines
content: the orientations of magnetic dipoles in a high-temperature magnetic material might be in a highly entropic, disordered state. If the material were allowed to cool, the dipoles would independently align to their local fields, and the entire material would tend toward a homogenous and steady globally-aligned state. The commonality between these examples is that their final states rest in energetic minima. In other words, it is thermodynamically favorable for them to come to rest, so from the

title: Hopfield Networks: Neural Memory Machines
content: moment each system’s external perturbations cease, they begin their respective state-trajectories toward the lowest energy possible. HNs implemented in the computer are not physical systems which evolve toward thermodynamically-stable states. However, because of the constraints built into the network, defined by their structure and update rules, they display analogous behavior. Remember, they were initially inspired by the Ising model. In fact, HNs have a scalar value, termed Energy, which

title: Hopfield Networks: Neural Memory Machines
content: monotonically decreases with each subsequent update generation. A HN’s state-trajectory over time can be thought of as a point descending an energy landscape; when the network converges to a memory, it has found itself in a ‘valley’ of the landscape, and will evolve no further unless disturbed. Fig 7. An example energy landscape – A Hopfield Nework’s ‘memory’ states are stable attractors. In the example above, there are many stable attractors, or valleys. Each attractor represents a memory, and

title: Hopfield Networks: Neural Memory Machines
content: the network state will evolve in the direction of whichever attractor is closest to the initial state (image by author) The beauty of HNs lies in the fact that, depending on learned weights, the respective attractors, or energetic minima, are adjustable. Any state of the system can be made, or learned, to be an attractor, and thus any state can be a learned memory. title: Hopfield Networks: Neural Memory Machines
content: Modern Hopfield Networks – If you’ve made it this far, you understand that the HNs which we’ve discussed thus far have neurons which occupy discrete binary states: -1 or 1. This is useful, but somewhat restrictive in terms of what information is possible to be efficiently stored within the network. Theoretically, a sufficiently large binary HN could store any information, but consider how many neurons you’d need to store even just one greyscale image. Say we had a 28×28 image in grayscale;

title: Hopfield Networks: Neural Memory Machines
content: grayscale is an image format which stores pixel values as integers between 0(black) and 255(white). If we have 28×28 = 784 pixels in our relatively small image, and we choose to represent each pixel’s grayscale value as an unsigned 8-bit integer, we’d require a HN with 6,272 neurons to fully represent the informational content of the image. For a larger image resolution, say 1,024×1,024, we’d need >8,000,000 neurons. Information in modern-day machine learning is rich in both content and

title: Hopfield Networks: Neural Memory Machines
content: dimension, and so its clearly an advantage to have neurons which can occupy continuous states, decreasing the number of neurons needed to represent memories, and vastly increasing the informational storage capacity of the network. Progress in the realm of continuous Hopfield Networks (CHNs) was introduced first in the 2020 paper Hopfield Networks is All You Need. CHNs offer a couple of advantages over classic binary HNs. As suggested by their name, the state of neurons in a CHNs are continuous,

title: Hopfield Networks: Neural Memory Machines
content: i.e. they are floats, rather than integers 0 or 1. So the state of a CHN at any given update generation is a vector of floating point numbers. This drastically increases the complexity of patterns which can be learned and retrieved by the network. In addition, the storage capacity of the network, as in how many distinct patterns it can remember and recall, is exponentially higher than in binary networks – binary Hopfield networks (BHNs) are prone to ‘spurious’ minima. If memories learned by a

title: Hopfield Networks: Neural Memory Machines
content: BHN are too similar, or if too many pattern vectors are learned, the network risks converging to an in-between memory, some combination of learned patterns; in other words, the network will fail to discriminate between patterns and becomes useless. In 2020 paper cited above, the authors propose a CHN architecture which offers some applicability to modern-day machine learning problems. Notably, the network proposed: converges in one step stores exponentially more patterns than a BHN is capable of

title: Hopfield Networks: Neural Memory Machines
content: aiding in classification tasks with rich and high-dimensional data I won’t cover the details of the paper here, but feel free to explore it yourself. The authors provide a use-case for their implementation, and show that, as a supplemental layer to a deep-learning architecture, CHNs perform better than other state-of-the-art algorithms in the complex task of immune repertoire classification. title: Unsupervised Learning: K-Means Clustering
content: Machine Learning Theory K-means clustering is an iterative algorithm that selects the cluster centers that minimize the within-cluster variance. Introduction In this article, I want to introduce one of the simplest data clustering algorithms, k-means clustering. It is an algorithm that often shows up in interviews to test your knowledge of fundamentals. After reading this article you’ll understand the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning, and the maths behind a simple data

title: Unsupervised Learning: K-Means Clustering
content: clustering model. Unsupervised Learning Many common machine learning problems fall into the supervised learning domain. Any problem to do with classification or regression often falls into supervised learning. Supervised learning problems consist of problems where we know the "labels" of our training data. If we know the labels, then the task consists of training some hidden function that can map our data matrix to the hidden labels. For example in a classifier, we know what training data

title: Unsupervised Learning: K-Means Clustering
content: belongs to what class, and so we train a function like a neural network to fit the data, and use the trained model to predict unseen data. In unsupervised learning, we don’t know the labels of our training data. We cannot create a direct mapping between inputs and outputs. The goal is therefore to learn to detect patterns in the data and exploit them. Data Clustering: K-Means Introduction to the problem Clustering algorithms are a type of unsupervised learning models. Their goal is to cluster

title: Unsupervised Learning: K-Means Clustering
content: the data into groups. Think of a classification problem where you know how many classes there are but your data is unlabeled. In k-means clustering, we assume we know how many groups there are, and then we cluster the data into that number of groups. The number of groups is denoted as "k", hence the name of the algorithm. Say we have the following problem: 3 Cluster problem (Image by author) We have a 2-dimensional dataset. The dataset appears to contain 3 clusters (we don’t know their true

title: Unsupervised Learning: K-Means Clustering
content: labels when training). We don’t know each individual datapoint’s class membership, but we do know that there are 3 groups in the system. Can we make an algorithm that determines which cluster each point belongs to? Formulation We are given the data matrix X. It is an Nxd matrix with N data points each with d dimensions (in our problem d = 2). We want to determine the class membership (rnk). This variable is 0 if the data point doesn’t belong to a cluster, and 1 otherwise. Here is an example:

title: Unsupervised Learning: K-Means Clustering
content: Class membership visualized (Image by author) Above is an example of what the vector of a data point and its class membership look like. The point belongs to cluster 3, so it rn3 is 1, the rest are 0. The goal is to find out rnk for all data points. Objective Function To train a machine learning model we often look for some sort of error function that we can minimize in order to train our model. In the case of k-means clustering, the goal is to find the cluster centers that minimize the within-

title: Unsupervised Learning: K-Means Clustering
content: cluster variance: If we minimize the objective function J, we are minimizing the square of the Euclidian distance between the chosen cluster center μ for that cluster. Image by Author So for each cluster, we look at the points that we think belong to that cluster, and we choose the cluster center that minimizes the squared of the Euclidian distance between the cluster center and all the points in the cluster. I’ve noted the Euclidian distance as the L2 norm in the image above. We can take the

title: Unsupervised Learning: K-Means Clustering
content: objective function shown above, differentiate with respect to the cluster centers and equate to 0 to find the cluster centers resulting in the minimum loss (the minimum within cluster variance). Derivation of optimal cluster centers. Note the sum over the cluster centers K goes when differentiating. In the derivation above we find the optimal cluster center (the one that minimizes the within cluster variance) is the mean of each cluster. This is an intuitive result. The point that will minimize

title: Unsupervised Learning: K-Means Clustering
content: variance in a cluster will be in the mean. k-means algorithm So we know that the optimal cluster center is the mean of each cluster, but we cannot calculate the mean of each cluster without knowing the class membership (rnk). To get around this we implement an iterative algorithm: k-means pseudo code (by Author) We start of by randomly initializing our cluster centers (Line 1). We can do this by picking k points at random. Then we assign each data point to the cluster center that is closest to

title: Unsupervised Learning: K-Means Clustering
content: it according to the Euclidian distance (Lines 7–10). We then update the cluster centers by computing the mean of each one (Lines 14–17). Finally, we repeat this until the cluster centers converge. Random initialization (Image by Author) In the image above 3 cluster centers have been initialized by picking 3 points at random. The colors represent which cluster center each data point is assigned to. The class membership rnk has been computed by calculating the Euclidian distance for each point to

title: Unsupervised Learning: K-Means Clustering
content: all 3 cluster centers, and picking the one closest to it. As you can see the cluster center that is furthest down takes up most of the data. The next step in the algorithm is to compute the mean of each cluster and to update the cluster centers. The orange and blue cluster centers won’t move much, but the green cluster center will move far down. After updating the cluster centers, we compute the class membership again, repeating until the points have converged: Converging from random

title: Unsupervised Learning: K-Means Clustering
content: initialization (GIF by Author) As you can see above the k-means algorithm finds the true cluster centers successfully. Problems with k-means clustering Dependence on Initialization A big problem with k-means clustering is its consistency. k-means isn’t very consistent due to its random initialization. The algorithm can produce very different results depending on where you initialize the cluster centers. k-means stuck over bad initialization (GIF by Author) In the GIF above the same model as

title: Unsupervised Learning: K-Means Clustering
content: before but with different initialization. The model is unsuccessful in finding the true cluster centers because of an unlucky initialization. The mean of the blue cluster gets stuck between two clusters, where as the orange and green cluster centers divide the third cluster. We Don’t Always Know K Since this is unsupervised learning we might not know the real number of clusters. This will also result in erroneous cluster centers. 4 Cluster centers (GIF by Author) The Data is Not Always Uniformly

title: Unsupervised Learning: K-Means Clustering
content: Distributed In k-means clustering, each data point is assigned to the cluster center that it is closest to. In a two dimensional space, the decision boundary between two cluster centers will be linear, and will not consider the shape of each distribution. This works well for distributions with no correlation like the ones we have shown so far. But if we introduce correlation in the data, k-means starts to underperform. Bivariate Gaussians and k-means (GIF by author) Take a look at the orange and

title: Unsupervised Learning: K-Means Clustering
content: blue clusters in the gif above. The blue cluster is eating into the orange one even though visually we can tell those points belong to the orange cluster. In k-means we do not consider correlations in the data, but there are other clustering techniques that do. If your data is normally distributed like the one above, k-means may not be the best clustering algorithm. Stay tuned for a future article on Gaussian Mixture Models! Conclusion This article intuitively explains k-means clustering, a

title: Unsupervised Learning: K-Means Clustering
content: simple data clustering algorithm. k-means clustering iteratively estimates the cluster centers of an unlabeled dataset that minimize the within-cluster variance. Since we don’t know the class membership, to compute the within-cluster variance, we first initialize the cluster centers at random, then expect the new cluster center of each cluster as the mean of the data points assigned to each cluster. k-means has big downsides which I highlight towards the end of the article, and in the future, I

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: caption | Photo by Anni Roenkae This continues a series of articles that build on each other. Please read my last article on Time Series Analysis and Logistic Regression. Alright, let us start with supervised learning. I covered some of this in my earlier articles but let me go over some specifics for this article. Supervised learning: learns from existing data which are categorized and labeled with predefined classes. Test data are labeled into these classes as well Well, this is true of all

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: types of learning. But, specifically, it has labeled predefined classes. That is the most important thing – supervised learning has something that is called an expert label. That’s a fancy word for meaning that it is labeled for an outcome; or for any given case, there is a known, desired outcome. Unsupervised learning (clustering) does not assume that it knows the answer. So clustering, for instance, will take a look at the data and partition the data, according to how the data are. Supervised

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: learning will partition the data according to the label. This is a big difference. An example of unsupervised learning is clustering. An example of supervised learning is regression, as I have written about before. For instance, in a regression model, we have X and Y, and we draw a best fit line through that. In this example, X are our inputs, and Y is the output. We can say this is supervised learning because Y is the expert label; the model is learning how to take X and come up with Y given

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: these expert labels. Examples: Fraud transaction: we know which transactions in the training data were fraud (1), and which were not (0) Readmission: we know which patients were readmitted to a hospital within a certain time window after discharge Recommendation: we know which items were presented to customers, and which items were clicked, added to the cart, or purchased A classic example is a spam filter Machine learning tasks have a variety of purposes. Here are a few examples of classic

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: machine learning tasks: identifying fraud, identifying readmission of patients, identifying recommendations like your typical Netflix machine learning case that is when you go on to Netflix, you get recommendations of movies that you will like; those movies are based on previous movies that you looked at and considering what other people liked when they had watched similar movies to the movies you watched, and what movies they watched, in addition to that. This is called a recommendation engine.

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: As an aside, this recommendation engine is sort of a gray area, that might not always be described as supervised learning, but I digress. A classic example of supervised learning is a spam filter. What does a spam filter do? It classifies between spam and no spam on your email. The way the model learned this is by someone, an "expert" – a human, who came by and marked various emails as spam or not spam. Then the emails and those labels were given to an algorithm that was expected to figure out

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: how to get from the email to that label on its own. This whole process is called supervised learning. Typical machine learning tasks: Classification: can we label the input? Regression: can we make a prediction? Recommendations: can we predict something based on user preference? Supervised learning has two important steps: first, you train a model, and then you test the model. It is very important to use unseen test data for testing your model. In previous articles, I wrote about supervised

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: learning, like with a regression, I did not use test data, and used training data to test the model. This is is bad, not a good thing to do. People do it on occasion, there are different reasons for doing it. There are very few legitimate reasons, but there are some. If you use training data to determine the accuracy of your model, then you are at best fooling yourself; and at worst, you are lying. So to test the model, you need to use so-called "unseen test data." Now, how do we create unseen

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: test data? Well, that is pretty simple. You just take your modeling data and split it into training data and test data: the test data is used for the testing of the model after the model has been trained on the training segment. What do we mean by learning? You use the data together with the algorithm to come up with a performance measure or to minimize a cost function – that is the other way of saying it. When you do that, then you will come up with a model with new operational data and you

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: will be able to get an answer. Fundamental assumption of learning A fundamental assumption of learning is that the distribution of training examples is identical to the distribution of test examples, including future unseen examples. More importantly, the distribution of training examples is similar enough to future examples. Given that they are future examples, they are unseen. If you want to have an accuracy measure, then that distribution should also be similar to the test examples. This

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: assumption is not a requirement. What is a requirement is that your test examples, for you to trust your accuracy, have to come from the same distribution as your future examples. Where your training examples came from is not important if you create a usable model. If your training examples come from a different distribution, more power to you. To be a valid measure, the test examples have to be similar enough to the examples that will be used in practice when it comes to operational data – when

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: it comes to operationalizing. Now strong violations to the above assumption will result in poor classification accuracy. Machine learning framework Image by author Training: given a training set of labeled examples {(x_1, y_1, … (x_n, y_n)}, estimate the prediction function (f) and parameters (Theta) which minimizes the prediction error on the training set Training function | Image by author Testing: apply (f) to a never before seen test example (x) and output the predicted value (y = f(x)) With

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: the overall machine learning framework, you give an X and you get back a Y. And there is going to be somewhat of an error because there is some random noise associated with everything. That means that the actual Y that you get is not going to be exactly the above function. Classification Workflow Classification workflow diagram | Image by author The most important thing is the data have to be split into a training set and test set. The model is developed in the training set, the model is

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: evaluated on the test set. Lastly, you get performance measures, also called accuracy measures. Here there are three performance measures: of which the performance measure called accuracy is probably the worst performance measure. Precision and recall are pretty good. There is a better one that is a hybrid of precision and recall, the F1 score. The reason I like it more is that it is sort of a hybrid between the recall and the precision. And you will want to have both good recall and precision.

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: If you have very good recall and very lousy precision or vice versa, your model is not worth much. There is an even better accuracy measure for binary classifications – the ROC AUC. So the AUC, area under the curve, of a ROC curve, is for classifications. The reason why it is better than the previous performance measures is that it is valid for all thresholds; whereas accuracy or precision presumes a threshold – typically it presumes a threshold of 0.5. Likewise, the F1 score also presumes a

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: threshold of 0.5. You could choose a different threshold, but most people would not assume that you would have chosen a different threshold. The reason why you choose a different threshold is that you may have a different purpose in mind, where you have false positives might be worse for you than false negatives, or vice versa. By being able to tune your threshold, you can trade those off. Many classifiers to choose from Linear Regression Logistic Regression Support Vector Machine (SVM) Neural

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: networks (ANN, CNN, RNN, DNN) Naive Bayes Bayesian network Randomized Forests (Random forests) Boosted Decision Trees (Gradient boosted trees) K-nearest neighbor (KNN) Here are so-called classifiers, algorithms used in supervised learning. KNN is generally considered your simplest concept and is often taught in classes like these because the algorithm is relatively simple: you can write out the algorithm from scratch. Boosted decision trees and randomized forests used to be your generally

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: favored machine learning classification algorithms. Today the "newest" types of algorithms are the neural nets. And when I say the newest, my statement is about five to 10 years old, depending on how you look at it. But up to about five years ago, Kaggle competitions were won by boosted decision trees and randomized forests. Now Kaggle competitions are being won by deep neural nets. So not neural nets, as such, but a more sophisticated version of neural nets called deep neural nets (DNN).

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: Logistic regression is everyone’s favorite – whenever you do a classification, you first do a logistic regression, always! Naive Bayes is a favorite too in that same sense. But logistic regression maybe even a little bit more so. So you always do logistic regression; not because you want to show off the results of the logistic regression. It is just that it is so robust and you know if you cannot get the logistic regression to work, you will not be able to get anything else to work either. So

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: logistic regression is the first thing you try to get to work. When that works, then you start becoming more daring and venture into some of these other algorithms listed above. Generalization Underfitting: model is too "simple" to represent all the relevant class characteristics – high training error and high validation error. Overfitting: model is too "complex" and fits irrelevant characteristics (noise) in the data – low training error and high validation error (big gap between training and

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: validation performance) Generalization means how well it works. As a good heuristic whenever you say generalization, you think of regularization. Why do this? Because the way you generalize a model is by regularizing the model. If you have a well-regularized model, it is presumably generalized. What does generalization mean? It means it will work under more than just minimal circumstances. Thus no overfitting has occurred. An underfit model is generally too simple and more work needs to be done

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: to extract information from it. But an overfit model is not generalized well enough and requires regularization. Common pitfalls in machine learning Overfitting Underfitting Data leakage: the creation of unexpected additional information in the training data, creating unrealistically good predictions. Leaking test data into training data. The inclusion of data not present in the model’s operational environment Rarely is underfitting a pitfall, maybe the usage of algorithms which are too

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: primitive and that results in sort of a way of underfitting because people might have stopped with logistic regression and they should have used a gradient boosted tree if you want to consider that a kind of underfitting. Overfitting is one of your big issues, as mentioned earlier. Now the next big issue is data leakage or proxy columns or proxies of any sort. These issues happen a lot. This concept is hard to understand, it is hard to explain, hard to teach why such things happen often unless

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: you have done this yourself. For example, where you have been looking at your data for a month, working with it, and only once your test results come back, and you see your test results for your machine learning algorithm like .97 on your accuracy. Only then do you realize, "Oh, I must have data leakage." Simply put – it is vanishingly rare that you get a model that good. Then you have to dissect your model, you have to find out why your model is too good to be true. And the reason your model is

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: too good to be true is usually because of data leakage. A real-life example: a prostate cancer model included a variable stating whether or not patients had prostate cancer surgery. A model cannot see the future, and the data for whether or not the patient had surgery should have been removed from the model for training. Confusion Matrix Encoding for the confusion matrix Here is an example of a confusion matrix. One important note about these confusion matrices is that they typically have the

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: true negative in the upper left and the true positive in the lower right. The reason why this is the case, nowadays, is because zero is less than one. Since true negatives are usually modeled as zeros, it makes numeric sense to list them first. When you have your actual versus your predicted classes reduced to the easiest format for a computer to understand them, then you have reduced them to zero and one. Since zero is smaller than one zero goes first and one goes second. Since zeros are

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: smaller than one, zeros go first also in the vertical dimension and then ones well. Zeros are typically associated with the absence of something and they are typically associated with a negative. Here a negative is not a bad thing – if I am COVID-19 negative, this means I do not have COVID, or at least my test came back negative for COVID. If I do not have COVID then this is what I call a true negative or 0 0. Likewise, the encoding of 1 1 would mean I do have COVID and I tested positive for it.

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: This is why true negatives and true positives are aligned this way: true negatives are in the upper left, true positives are in the lower right. This was not always the case – it used to be the other way around! But this is what you see most of the time these days. And that just has to do with the ordering of zero and one! Precision and recall are important concepts to understand but are beyond the scope of this article. As I mentioned above, I prefer the F1 score, the harmonic mean (as opposed

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: to the arithmetic mean) of precision and recall as my "accuracy" metric over choosing either one. But the best performance measure for classification is the ROC curve. The Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve is great for classifications. I believe it is the most important accuracy measure but sometimes it cannot be used. There are reasons for that, but generally, the ROC curve is what you want to use. The reason why you want to use the ROC curve is that it considers all thresholds. To

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: illustrate why this is important, consider this hypothetical interview question: give people numbers for false positive, for true positive, false negative, and true negative – there are there 10 in each of those. So that would give you about the worst accuracy score possible: 0.5 as an aside consider that if your model is .01 accurate, then just switch the labels for your 0 and 1 classes and suddenly your model is .99 accurate But if you look at the probabilities, the probabilities for the true

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: positives and the true negatives: are all-around zero and one – meaning they are good. The probabilities of the false positives and false negatives are all around 0.5, which means they are really bad. This means the errors are shaky, and the correct results are very good or very secure; thus you will get a higher ROC AUC score for that! You will never see anything like that with any of these other accuracy measures because they do not consider probabilities. They only consider the boolean

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: outcomes: is it a true positive or is it not a true positive? Naive Bayes Some properties of Naive Bayes models are Do not require a prior Computational complexity is linear in the number of parameters/features Requires minimal data to produce models that generalize well Have a simple and inherent regularization Some applications: Document classification SPAM detection Image classification Yes, the Bayes in Naive Bayes does refer to Bayes theorem, which I have previously written about. There is

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: also a very clear link between Bayes theorem and Naive Bayes model. However, the presumption with the Naive Bayes model is that the individual dimensions are independent, or naive. That means the important part about Bayes theorem, where you can relate the probability of A to the probability of B or the intersection is not needed. What we have here in the naive consideration is that we say that these probabilities are independent of each other. Thus the conditional probability basically goes

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: away. This is the "naive" in Naive Bayes – acting as if your data dimensions are independent. If your data dimensions are not independent, then your Naive Bayes will not work well. A surprising result, or at least surprising if you focus too much on this independence requirement, is that the Naive Bayes model will still work pretty well if your dimensions are not fully independent. Regardless my point is that some of the most difficult parts in considering Bayes theorem become very simple with

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: Naive Bayes; because you presume that the probabilities are independent of each other – thus no conditional probabilities need to be calculated or presumed. The dimensional independence presumption allows you to multiply probabilities with each other, which greatly simplifies the computations needed to train and test the model. Like how a logistic regression is used as a classifier, you would not be wrong to call it, instead, a logistic classifier. Thus a better name for Naive Bayes might be the

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: Naive Probability Model, to distance itself from the conditional probabilities inherent in Bayes theorem. Pitfalls of Naive Bayes Multiplication of small probabilities leads to floating-point underflow. This problem is corrected by computing with the log probabilities, ln(p) If there are no samples/data then p(xj | Ck) = 0, leading to the product of the probabilities to be 0. A Laplace smoother is used to ensure that all p(xj | Ck) > 0 Collinear features do not exhibit independence. Ideally,

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: such features should be removed from the dataset to prevent problems with the model Regularization is generally a minor issue with Naive Bayes models, as uninformative features tend to a uniform distribution, which does not affect the outcome Types of Naive Bayes Models Now that we have looked into the basics of a Naive Bayes model, let us look at some specific formulations. It is important to keep in mind that a specific naive Bayes model is required for each class of problems. The multinomial

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: naive Bayes classifier is a widely used form of the model. The multinomial classifier finds the most likely class from multiple possibilities. title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: probability that document D has topic C based on the occurrence of the words {w1, w2,…, wn}, using the following relationship: Credit: Wikipedia In this document classification example, you have a variety of documents, a so-called corpus of documents. That means you have a collection of documents and these documents are labeled in some way. First, a document is given an "expert" label (spam or not spam). After applying labels what you do is you create a column out of every word, which means

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: every word becomes a boolean column, like with one-hot encoding. You repeat this process for every word in that document. There are ways of reducing the number of columns but my point is that Naive Bayes is very useful for document classification. Now, what are some examples of this? For instance, is this document plagiarized or not? Is this document fake news or not? Is this spam or not? The reason why Naive Bayes is a favored method is that the model does not mind the huge number of

title: An Introduction to Supervised Learning
content: dimensions. There can be some performance degradation or fidelity degradation resulting in the classifier not having as good accuracy with huge numbers of data dimensions. But, there are ways of removing superfluous inputs. Computationally speaking, this is very quick hence why it is a favorite choice for document classification. title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: Data Science Interview In this blog posrt, we are covering another type of interview that an aspiring data scientist has to learn to crack: the statistics interview. A statistics interview is a technical interview that evaluates your ability to actually do your job as a data scientist. If you do not ace this interview, you will have a hard time convincing a company that you are a capable data scientist. The first step to acing any interview is knowing what to expect. Statistics is a broad

title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: subject, so this post will break down what areas of statistics a data scientist is expected to know for interviews and what types of questions will be asked. We will also discuss tips and general advice throughout. I also have a video on this subject if you would prefer to get the information that way! Let’s start with what areas of statistical knowledge a statistics interview will cover. Table of Contents Areas of Knowledge Probability Hypothesis Testing Regression Types of Questions Conceptual

title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: Questions Questions Involving Calculations Coding Questions Conclusion Areas of Knowledge In a statistics interview, you naturally have to demonstrate a lot of technical knowledge, but that does not mean that you need to be prepared to answer any and all questions related to statistics. For data scientists, a statistics interview will typically focus on three areas of knowledge: Probability Hypothesis Testing Regression Probability For probability questions, you should expect to be asked about

title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: probability basics, conditional probability, and probability distribution. Probability basics includes expectation, variance, permutation, and combinations, etc. For conditional probability, you will need to know Bayes’ rule, and for probability distribution, you need to be familiar with some commonly used discrete and continuous distributions, such as binomial, normal, and long-tailed distribution. This may sound like a lot, but probability is typically the area of knowledge for which you will

title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: need the most in-depth knowledge for interviews. There are therefore a lot of things the interviewer could ask you about, and besides, it is always better to over-prepare than to under-prepare. Hypothesis Testing Moving on to hypothesis testing, for statistics interviews you need to be aware of both the terminology, such as power, p-value, and confidence interval, and the different kinds of testing methods, parametric tests, such as z-test, t-test, and non-parametric tests, such as chi-squared

title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: test, and more. Regression The final area of knowledge you need for statistics interviews is regression. For regression, you need to be familiar with linear and multiple regression. Of the three areas, regression will likely appear the least in interviews, but you still need to make sure you are comfortable with it. So probability, hypothesis testing, and regression are the areas on which you will be questioned in an interview. Now that we know what subjects the questions will cover, let’s

title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: discuss the types of questions you can expect. Types of Questions There are three different formats that questions take in a statistics interview: Conceptual Questions Questions Involving Calculations Coding Questions Understanding what types of questions you will be asked is crucial in understanding how to prepare and how to answer. Let’s take a closer look at each type. Conceptual Questions As the name suggests, conceptual questions are more interested in your ability to explain concepts than

title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: your ability to do math with those concepts. We can further break this category down into two styles: explaining to a technical audience and explaining to a non-technical audience. Before we dive into the different approaches for explaining concepts to a technical versus a non-technical audience, what exactly are conceptual questions? Let’s look at some examples of conceptual questions from each of the areas of knowledge you can expect in a statistics interview. Probability: What is the

title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: distribution of average time spent per user? Hypothesis Testing: Explain p-value and confidence interval to a non-technical audience. Regression: What are the assumptions of linear regression? As you can see from the examples, conceptual questions ask you to define terms and show an understanding of what these things mean in a real-world context. You will likely be asked to explain a term or concept, sometimes for a non-technical audience. Explaining a concept is a bit of a vague request though,

title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: so what should you include in your answers to these conceptual questions? Explaining to a Technical Audience Let’s start by looking at some steps for explaining concepts to a technical audience. It can be easy to dismiss the importance of this as a data scientist. After all, if the audience has a technical background, they should understand your explanation with no problems right? While a technical audience should have an easier time following the terminology and general idea of your

title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: explanations, if your answer is not organized or if it deals with a more obscure concept, it can still be difficult to follow. You still need to take steps to ensure that you can explain the concepts clearly. Here are the steps I recommend: Start with some context. When or where is this terminology used? Define that concept. Even when explaining to a technical person, you want to keep the definition easy to understand. Try to not sound like a high-level textbook. Your ability to explain things

title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: in simple terms shows a higher level of understanding. For concepts that can be represented by numbers, you might want to explain what changes in value mean. What does it mean when this concept has a larger or smaller value? This step is optional. You can finish by talking about how this concept is applied in practice. Think about questions such as why is this concept widely used or why is it important to data science. To see these steps in action, I recommend checking out one of my videos on

title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: how to explain the top 5 statistical concepts in interviews. Explaining to a Non-Technical Audience These steps hopefully give you some clear talking points and structure when you are asked to explain or define a concept to a technical audience, but how does a non-technical audience differ? As you saw earlier in our examples, you may be asked to explain a concept in layman terms or to a non-technical audience, this requires you to explain things more intuitively. Using examples and analogy is a

title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: great way to explain terminology to a non-technical audience. Try to make connections to things that a layman would be more familiar with to explain what is unfamiliar. It is also crucial to avoid using technical terms when explaining things to a non-technical audience. For example, If you use terms like hypothesis testing, null hypothesis, or alternative hypothesis when explaining the concept of the power of a test, you will only confuse your audience. With all conceptual questions, the goal

title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: should be to keep your explanations clear and structured. Remember that even with a technical audience, you want your explanation to be as easy to understand as possible as this shows a deeper understanding of the concepts. Questions Involving Calculations Understanding the concepts and terminology is wonderful and necessary for a data scientist, but you also have to be able to do the math that goes along with those concepts. A statistics interview will include questions that involve actual

title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: calculations. Questions involving calculations could require you to simply know what to use to solve a problem. For example, a conditional probability question might require you to use Bayes’ rule to calculate it, but the question itself may not mention Bayes’ rule. This is evaluating if you can correctly identify what methods and steps you need to solve a particular problem, basically if you know HOW to do the problem. A question involving calculations could go much further though. It could ask

title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: you to write the equation and provide the exact answer. This would be evaluating not only if you know how to do the problem but also if you actually can do the math correctly. For example, the problem might say "We have a total of 100 coins, which includes 99 fair coins and 1 biased coin that has a probability of getting heads 100%. If you choose a random coin and flip it 10 times and all 10 times are heads, what’s the probability that the coin is the biased coin?" This problem not only requires

title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: you to know that you need to use Bayes’ rule, but you also have to find the numerical answer here. Some more examples of questions that involve calculations would be: "What’s the probability of getting two heads among 10 tosses of a fair coin?" "Given two groups of users, compare the click-through rates and draw conclusions as to whether the two click-through rates are the same". "Can you lay out the testing steps and draw conclusions?" The first question is an example of a question dealing with

title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: probability distribution, and the second is hypothesis testing. The final example is something you might be asked after getting the results of another question. I recommend this video for a better look at hypothesis testing questions. To summarize, questions involving calculations are thus one way that the interviewer evaluates whether you can deliver on your knowledge. These questions are an opportunity to show that you have not only knowledge but skills as well. The final type of question, the

title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: coding question, gives you even more opportunity to demonstrate your skills. Coding Questions If conceptual questions are all about your understanding of concepts then coding questions are all about your implementation skills. These questions will require you to not only know about theories but to also implement those theories. For example, a coding question that deals with probability might ask you to design and run a coin simulation problem. Check out this video for a more in-depth look at

title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: this type of problem. Another example would be a hypothesis testing coding question, which will likely have you writing code in R or Python to calculate the results. These examples and indeed all coding questions, let you demonstrate an ability to get results. Understanding what to do is one thing, but showing that you can do it is crucial for acing an interview. Of course, the best way to prepare for coding questions is to practice coding. I recommend the 10 days of statistics by HackerRank to

title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: get started on some statistics problems. Conclusion Generally speaking, statistics interviews are a very skill-based type of interview. You need to be prepared to show thorough knowledge and capability in these interviews. So to recap, there are three areas of statistical knowledge you will need to prepare for in interviews as a data scientist: Probability Hypothesis Testing Regression You may notice that we did not talk about causal inference, even though it is a domain closely related to

title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: statistics. If you would like to learn about causal inference in data science interviews, make sure to subscribe to this channel to get updates on future content. Besides the three areas of knowledge there are also three types of questions you can expect in a statistics interview: Conceptual questions Questions involving calculations Coding questions All together these three types of questions evaluate both your understanding and skill with statistical problems you would face as a data

title: Cracking Statistics Interviews for Data Scientists
content: scientist. With this outline, you now know what you need to know and prepare to ace statistics interviews as a data scientist. Good luck! Thanks for Reading! title: A Curated Question List for Data Science Candidates To Ask During the Interview
content: Career Motivation Data scientist is one of the most compelling jobs and still has growth as long as the companies still want to utilize their data with the business very well. However, the hype around the data market makes every job posting and requirement look very similar. Therefore, it is hard for the candidate to distinguish what data scientists do in day-to-day operations. This problem leads to the misalignment between the data science candidate’s hope and the company’s expectations,

title: A Curated Question List for Data Science Candidates To Ask During the Interview
content: resulting in a short-term resignation of the valuable data scientist. After several personal interview experiences, I concluded that we, as data science candidates, sometimes didn’t ask a sufficient amount of important questions to verify that what we expect in daily life is the same as the one the company wants. Also, when you make a final judgment, you may miss some critical decision variables that make the evaluation not complete holistically. For example, almost 80% of the interview time is

title: A Curated Question List for Data Science Candidates To Ask During the Interview
content: to checking whether the candidate had enough technical skills to deliver the solution to the company. In the end, we only had 10 to 15 minutes to ask the question back to the interviewer, and sometimes it’s capable of only 2 to 3 questions, and that’s all. However, with only a limited time and exhausted state after the technical interview, it is easy for the candidate to forget to ask the question you must know to make a career move decision. I found this problem from time to time, both myself

title: A Curated Question List for Data Science Candidates To Ask During the Interview
content: and my friends and colleagues who strive for their dream job. That’s why I write this article to walk you through the career aspects of data science and would like to give you the curated list of questions I think you should ask during the interview to reduce the risk of making a terrible decision before changing a career. 1. Data Science Projects & Operations When I started my data science career, I was the same as other data science enthusiasts who tried to land or switch a job to the field

title: A Curated Question List for Data Science Candidates To Ask During the Interview
content: without caring about what kind of business function I had to deal with. If you are lucky enough, you will land the job you will engage with. However, it could turn to other ways around as well. I found that to make a career move without thoroughly checking this topic is a big mistake. 1.1 Operations 🏃🏻 ‍♂️ What you do in daily life is the most important thing. First, you have to verify the day-to-day tasks you may face during the interview. Curated questions Can you walk me through the days of

title: A Curated Question List for Data Science Candidates To Ask During the Interview
content: data scientists at your company? – I prefer to hear the bad and tedious parts of day-to-day life rather than the exciting ones if possible. How many data scientists involving in one project? – this question is to check how to organization operates the data science team (a lone wolf embedded in a specific business unit or a center of excellence model) What is usually the period of data science project your organization achieved in the past (1 to 3 months or 6 to 12 months)? – In cases, you get

title: A Curated Question List for Data Science Candidates To Ask During the Interview
content: real bored quickly. Do you have a specific project management team for user requests, or is it a data scientist who self-manages the project? – Giving you a view of how many meetings you will have to handle during the day. How much time do you have to spend on the meeting or ad-hoc analysis? – Will you live your life peacefully or have to take a sprint every day at work. Honestly hope the interviewer tells you the truth, or you have to find an insider who can give you feedback about it. What is

title: A Curated Question List for Data Science Candidates To Ask During the Interview
content: the current size of the data team (both DS, DE, MLE, etc.), and how do you think it will become in the next 1, 3, and 5 years? – To check how vital the data team is in the near future and how much workload you have to handle if you move to this position. Some questions are tough to answer directly by the interviewer, so you may have to find the previous employee or a person in the current team to check the feedback. This part will clarify and can be used to compare with your current organization

title: A Curated Question List for Data Science Candidates To Ask During the Interview
content: whether it’s matched with your personal preference. You may not get all the answers at once but try your best. These answers are an essential part for to make a final decision. 1.2 Projects 🛠 The following essential topic is what kind of project you will involve with. In my opinion, we can divide the data science projects into two categories which are value creation and business function. These categories lead to different day-to-day life you will face during the working journey. Value creation

title: A Curated Question List for Data Science Candidates To Ask During the Interview
content: Value creation is the domain where we divide the projects whether revenue generation, cost-saving, or innovative solutions. Your project is a broad range of variety, and you will do whatever to drive the business towards any of the mentioned domains. Here is an example of the project you may work on in each Revenue generation – Propensity model, Product recommendation, Customer lifetime value, Retention rate improvement, Conjoint analysis, etc. Cost-saving – Supply chain optimization,

title: A Curated Question List for Data Science Candidates To Ask During the Interview
content: Route/Working shift scheduling, Automated financial reports, Digital marketing optimization, Demand forecasting, etc. Innovative solutions – Improving the KYC (Know your client) process with facial recognition, a Human-like chatbot for answering repetitive questions, etc. You may notice that if you are in the organization with this choice of data science operation, you will have a chance to do many areas of the project and expand your knowledge across the different business functions. Business

title: A Curated Question List for Data Science Candidates To Ask During the Interview
content: function A business function is another way to separate data science tasks. For example, it could be Sales & Marketing, Strategy, Risk, Operations, Supply chains, Fraud, Finance, Human resources, etc. Your project would dedicate to a specific business unit, and you will become a specialist within those areas. Here is an example of a project in marketing. Sales & Marketing – Propensity model, Digital marketing optimization, Product recommendation, Marketing mix modeling, etc. Risk – Probability

title: A Curated Question List for Data Science Candidates To Ask During the Interview
content: to default model, Fraud & Anomaly detection, Reject inference model, etc. Supply chains & Operation – Routing optimization for warehousing, Demand forecasting for inventory, Working shift scheduling, etc. If you know what you like and want to do, it’s easier to apply for the company with the business function strategy. You will have a chance to do what you love day in, day out. Curated questions ⭐️ What will be the assigned project if I get selected for this position, both short and long term (3

title: A Curated Question List for Data Science Candidates To Ask During the Interview
content: months to 1 year)? – This is a must question. Some companies don’t even know at the time they are hiring you what project you would be assigned to. Can you explain the kind of project the data science team dealing with, whether it’s value creation or business function basis? – To give a clear view of the next project you possibly will have a chance to work on. If you don’t have enough time for the interview, the star question is the most important one I recommend you to ask your hiring manager.

title: A Curated Question List for Data Science Candidates To Ask During the Interview
content: I found out recently that even though I can work on any data science project that the company gives to me, there is still a project that matches my inner passion the most. If you can find out that passion sooner. I’m sure that you have a brighter future await forward. To be honest, I just recently realized what project I would love to do after 4 years of working in this field. Unless you try everything like mine, I’m not sure what is the best way to find it out. 2. Performance Evaluation After

title: A Curated Question List for Data Science Candidates To Ask During the Interview
content: you set up your foundational understanding of the operation and project, performance evaluation is the next dimension you should be aware of. We always heard that many data science use cases don’t successfully deliver and deploy to the production stage. There are so many reasons why it’s difficult to deploy and maintain the machine learning model in live production, and it will take up a massive amount of resources to operate the system. And that may not be your fault. However, you have to know

title: A Curated Question List for Data Science Candidates To Ask During the Interview
content: how the hiring manager evaluates your performance at the beginning. So it’s critical to know that what you do during the year is a part of your year-end evaluation. If your manager only cares about the KPIs (result) and doesn’t care about the effort on experimentations (how you spend your time). That’s fine if you know it from the first day of work, not after you finish one year doing it and find that it doesn’t account in your performance review. Various hiring managers have their style to

title: A Curated Question List for Data Science Candidates To Ask During the Interview
content: evaluate the subordinate. Whether your hiring manager has a background in the data affects how they review and assess the data scientist’s performance. You have to carefully evaluate their perspective before joining the organization because I would say it’s impossible to convince them at the end of the year to change the way they evaluate your performance. The worst case is that you may spend one year of frustration without receiving the reward you deserve. Curated questions How do you evaluate

title: A Curated Question List for Data Science Candidates To Ask During the Interview
content: the data scientist’s performance? – the fundamental question I think we should know is how the hiring manager thinks about the data science task. What are the KPIs or OKRs that you usually monitor and expect data scientists to be responsible for it as well? – It’s easier to know the target KPIs to align our future project. For example, some hiring managers will have a non-financial related target like the number of experiments which is quite good for DS sometimes. Will you evaluate the

title: A Curated Question List for Data Science Candidates To Ask During the Interview
content: performance based on the KPIs only or consider the experimentation efforts as well? – To check what is critical to delivering, whether it’s multiple ad-hoc support or the single end-to-end data science model deployment. Will the ad-hoc analysis and maintaining part of the pipeline take into account? – There is always an unexpected task that we need to deliver in day-to-day life, and we should know how important it is so that we can plan a proper amount of time to do it. 3. Career Prosperity

title: A Curated Question List for Data Science Candidates To Ask During the Interview
content: Moving a career often has an opportunity cost. You would realize the benefit of your package only if you have been working throughout the full fiscal year. Also, you may be labeled as a job hopper if you have multiple moving career paths within a short time. These reasons lead to the fact that all we need is a peaceful workplace to settle down for a while. And to know if this is the right place, you can only assess it in the interview time. content: interview like this.
